She turned back to Shen Weici: “Zhao-zhao has always been straightforward by nature. In the future, when you are out and about, give way to her more often. If another incident like this occurs — if it grows into a fuss and gives the other branches cause to talk about the Second Branch — then I truly will not let it pass.”

Shen Weici obediently nodded: “Weici understands her place. She knows she cannot compare to Second Elder Sister, and in the future will keep her distance so as not to cause any friction.”

At that, Shen Zhaozhao shot to her feet and marched up to stand directly in front of Shen Weici, glaring at her: “What do you mean by that? Are you saying I’m being unreasonable and deliberately picking fights with you?”

Shen Weici met Shen Zhaozhao’s eyes calmly: “I would not dare. I simply know my own situation — I know Second Elder Sister would rather not see me. I would never go out of my way to put myself in front of her.”

Shen Zhaozhao gave a light sniff: “Good that you know it.”

Once they were outside Madam Wen’s courtyard, Yue Deng asked: “How much longer is the young miss going to endure this?”

Shen Weici was quiet for a moment: “My marriage rests in Second Madam’s hands. Although Father is now trying to find a match for me, even if one is settled, the matchmakers will still come to Second Madam first. I don’t want anything to go wrong.”

“If Second Madam were to interfere, she is my nominal stepmother — she truly could arrange any marriage she pleased. She has never wished me well, so what kind of family would she find for me?”

Yue Deng grew immediately worried: “What if Second Madam finds out about the arrangement with Master Zhang and puts her foot down?”

Shen Weici looked at Yue Deng: “It depends on whether Father is willing to stand up for me. Or perhaps even if Second Madam were truly difficult, Father wouldn’t be able to help — in which case I’d have no choice but to let word spread.”

“Madam Wen would earn herself a reputation for being cruel to her charges. Let’s see if she can still make things hard for me after that.”

Yue Deng asked again: “But what if Second Madam is determined regardless? I can see that the Second Master is also afraid of her...”

Shen Weici looked down at the hem of her skirt as branches swept past it: “Then I will have to think of another way.”

After returning, Shen Weici reclined on the daybed for another short nap.

In the afternoon, it had barely passed the appointed hour when Yue Deng came rushing in from outside, her face bright with excitement: “Young Miss, the Second Master’s man is asking you to come to the study!”

Shen Weici’s hand paused. She set down her brush and, for once, went to sit before the dressing table and let Yue Deng tidy her appearance.

Shen Weici had always been born beautiful, and even without ornate hairpins she was a charming, alluring sight that was difficult to look away from.

Yue Deng helped her put on the silver earrings she had brought from Yuyang, and smiled: “The young miss is lovely even without any adornment.”

Shen Weici smiled in reply and led Yue Deng out.

Following the maidservant to Tingzhu Pavilion, the girl at the gate spotted Shen Weici approaching from a distance and hurried inside to announce her, then came back out and said softly: “Please go in, miss — the Master is waiting inside.”

Shen Weici nodded and quietly lifted the curtain to enter.

Incense burned in the study, and she could hear a warm, unhurried voice inside.

She gathered her hands and passed through the inner screen, stepping into the room — and found a young man in dark-green robes standing with his back to her, upright as a stalk of bamboo, in wide-cut garments and a jade hairpin. He was saying with a smile: “I came upon this calligraphy copy quite by chance. I have already worked through it thoroughly — if it is to Minister Shen’s liking, I would be happy to give it to you.”

Shen Rongsheng replied: “My invitation today was no more than a passing impulse. Your father and I are old friends, and I have always felt an affinity for you — I simply wanted to spend a little time in conversation with a young man like yourself. Please keep the item.”

Hearing this, Shen Weici glanced once more at that upright back, then stepped forward with her eyes lowered and called out softly: “Father.”

Shen Rongsheng smiled warmly at Shen Weici’s arrival and beckoned her over: “You’ve come at a perfect moment. Were you not just saying you wanted to study Master Liang’s style? Zhang Er-lang has a fine hand — his calligraphy is of the proper tradition. Come and have a look.”

Shen Weici felt the other man’s gaze turn toward her. She kept her eyes lowered and walked obediently to her father’s side.

Shen Rongsheng looked at his daughter, then said pleasantly to Zhang Yuanheng: “This is the daughter I only recently brought back into the family.”

“Her mother passed away long ago. She took after her mother’s constitution — always somewhat delicate — and has been raised on an estate in the countryside. Now that she is about to come of age, I’ve brought her home at last.”

He turned to Shen Weici: “Weici, this is Zhang Er-lang. You may call him Master Zhang.”

Shen Weici finally lifted her eyes to take a brief look at Zhang Yuanheng, then lowered them again and greeted him softly: “Master Zhang.”

Zhang Yuanheng could not help but let his gaze settle on Shen Weici, who stood at Shen Rongsheng’s side.

She wore a rose-pink skirt, her eyes cast gently downward — yet at the outer corners of those eyes, a delicate hint of allure curled upward, and just above, a single dark beauty mark. Her nose was elegant and straight, her brows painted as though brushed on. Her face was lovely in the way of a melon-seed — round and smooth — yet suffused with a gentle, graceful warmth.

She was like boundless mountains and misty waters, touched by a single streak of pure white moonlight.

Her voice was soft and warm, the kind that easily stirred something in a listener.

He had come today partly because his father was close with Minister Shen, and partly because, at his age, marriage was indeed something to be considered. He had simply been too preoccupied with his official career before, and with no woman in his heart, he had set the matter aside — he had felt no great urgency to start a family.

But when his father brought it up again this time, he thought he might as well come and see. There was no harm in it.

He had not anticipated, however, that after this one meeting he would find himself unable to look away — that the sight of her, head bowed in quiet grace, would make his heart quicken.

chapters.title: Practicing Calligraphy
chapters.content:
The room was very quiet, filled with a gentle fragrance.

Though Zhang Yuanheng had been momentarily dazzled, he was well-mannered and composed, and did not look at her for long. He returned her greeting with a smile: “Miss Shen.”

Shen Weici found his voice warm and pleasant — the voice of someone with a very even temper. She lifted her head and met his clear, unclouded eyes. There was none of the lecherous look she had grown accustomed to from men back in Yuyang when they saw her.

Instead, he was candid and courteous. A single plain jade hairpin was all he wore, and it only made him look more refined — a handsome young gentleman one might pass on the road.

She was already favorably impressed.

Shen Rongsheng said to Shen Weici: “Since you’re here, why don’t you grind the ink? Let Zhang Er-lang write something for you to study — watch how he does it, and learn from him.”

Shen Weici glanced at the paper already spread on the desk, where a line of seven-character verse had been written. The brushwork was neat and practiced, the strokes sharply skilled — identical in spirit to the calligraphy copy beside it. She was quietly impressed.

She had once tried to copy Master Liang’s style herself, but perhaps owing to her weak foundation, she could only write small regular script. The moment any flowing quality entered the strokes, no matter how hard she tried, the result fell far short. She genuinely wanted to learn.

She moved to the desk and began grinding the ink with care, all the while aware of Zhang Yuanheng’s eyes on her.

Zhang Yuanheng watched those slender, delicate fingers — pale as mutton-fat jade, seemingly all fine bones — and felt an involuntary tenderness.

He had never encountered a woman like her. The capital, being in the north, tended to produce tall, robust women. Though Shen Weici was not short by any standard, she was on the small side compared to the women of the capital — yet that snow-white, porcelain smoothness of her skin was rarely seen.

The ink was ground. Zhang Yuanheng had a mind to show himself to advantage before her, and so he took up the brush and wrote slowly, stroke by stroke — as though making it easier for her to follow.

From the corner of his eye he caught a glimpse of pink-clad fabric, and glancing further, he saw that Shen Weici was indeed watching his brushwork with genuine attention. His palm grew warm, and for once he felt strangely nervous.

Zhang Yuanheng was writing a line from the Jinsi Lu — he had been reading that book recently and wrote a passage at random. It was, as always, fine calligraphy.

Shen Weici watched with full concentration, tracing the strokes in her mind — and then Zhang Yuanheng suddenly held the brush out to her with a smile: “Miss Shen, would you like to try?”

Zhang Yuanheng’s smile was too warmly gentle. Shen Weici felt a faint shyness and reached out to take the brush from him, watching as he stepped aside and thoughtfully spread a fresh sheet of paper for her before she could think to decline.

Shen Weici’s calligraphy had not been the finest at the village school, but it was strict and neat — extraordinarily tidy. The women’s teacher had once told her to write more loosely, but she was always too cautious, too afraid of ruining a character.

The brush still held the warmth of Zhang Yuanheng’s hand. Shen Weici, anxious not to embarrass herself, wrote with full concentration.

Shen Rongsheng glanced over, and though he had been a little worried it might look clumsy, he was pleasantly surprised to find it had something of its own character. While it lacked Zhang Yuanheng’s seasoned authority, for a young woman to produce work of this quality was more than admirable.

He looked at his daughter’s profile and thought, against his will, of a woman he had long pushed to the back of his mind. She had raised their daughter remarkably well. Even Zhao-zhao could not produce calligraphy as fine as this.

Zhang Yuanheng studied Shen Weici’s brushwork and felt his regard for her deepen by several degrees. The style was somewhat different from his own, but they came from the same tradition. Other than a slight tentativeness, there was nothing to fault.

He picked up a fresh brush, dipped it in ink, and went to stand beside Shen Weici to show her how a particular dot should fall: “If you let the brush turn like this, the character comes alive — it becomes something distinct from the regularity of small standard script.”

Shen Weici tried to imitate the way he brought the brush down for that dot, studying him with great earnestness.

Shen Rongsheng watched them from the side, a satisfied smile spreading across his face. The two of them standing at the window looked like a well-matched pair. If this match could be made, it would be his way of making amends to Shen Weici’s mother.

At last, as the sky began to darken, Zhang Yuanheng took his leave. Before departing, he placed the calligraphy copy in Shen Weici’s hands and said, looking at her gentle face: “When you have time, copy it. If you have any questions, write to me — I will always write back.”

Shen Weici looked at the copy in her hands, then back at Zhang Yuanheng: “I cannot accept something from Master Zhang. Please take it back.”

Zhang Yuanheng smiled: “A thing like this belongs with whoever needs it most. For it to end up in Third Miss’s hands is its good fortune — a fitting use.”

Autumn evenings darkened quickly. Zhang Yuanheng stood in the gathering dusk, holding a lantern, his eyes carrying a calm stillness that put those who looked at him at ease — one could only think of a man of deep refinement and quiet elegance.

Shen Rongsheng smiled beside him: “Since Zhang Er-lang has given it to you, go ahead and accept it.”

Shen Weici could not well refuse any longer. She reached out and took the copy, saying softly: “Thank you, Master Zhang.”

Zhang Yuanheng looked into Shen Weici’s eyes. The lamplight played between them, and in her dark pupils it was like watching fireworks unfold — his heart stirred.

Shen Rongsheng asked Shen Weici to head back first while he said a few more words to Zhang Yuanheng.

Shen Weici glanced at Zhang Yuanheng, then lowered her eyes and her gaze and left, clutching the calligraphy copy to her chest.

The moment she was gone, Shen Rongsheng looked at Zhang Yuanheng with a smile. He dispensed with all pleasantries and asked directly: “What do you make of my daughter?”

Zhang Yuanheng could not help but turn to watch the retreating figure of Shen Weici until she disappeared. Even now he could faintly catch the trace of her soft fragrance.

His expression turned serious as he looked at Shen Rongsheng: “Third Miss Shen is gracious, dignified, and of rare beauty — I would not presume to offer more than that.”

Shen Rongsheng smiled a little: “Weici has suffered some hardships since she was small. She is a good child — one I hold dear.”

“If your intentions are sincere, come to propose early, and treat her well in the years to come.”

Zhang Yuanheng heard these words, deliberated briefly, and then clasped his hands before Shen Rongsheng in a respectful bow: “My feelings for Third Miss Shen are genuine. However, I do not yet know her feelings toward me — to send a formal proposal immediately would seem rather presumptuous.”

“Furthermore, my mother is currently at a villa on the outskirts of town, tending to my grandmother’s illness, and has not yet returned home — she cannot come in person just yet.”

“Minister Shen, please allow me a little more time. If Third Miss Shen is willing to marry me, I will come to propose at the latest after the New Year.”

Shen Rongsheng smiled at the young man before him — upright and well-mannered, accomplished in appearance, and destined for a distinguished official career. For the Marquis household, such a match would also be advantageous. That Zhang Yuanheng could be pleased with Shen Weici was the very best possible outcome.

He took Zhang Yuanheng by both arms, treating him as one of his own: “Your father and I are old friends, and I have long known your character — naturally I trust you with my daughter. I would not have specially invited you today otherwise.”

“If you are fond of her, I will betroth my daughter to you — and Weici will certainly agree.”

Zhang Yuanheng gave another solemn bow: “I will not disappoint you.”

Shen Rongsheng smiled and personally moved to see Zhang Yuanheng out.

But before they had gone more than a few steps, an attendant hurried to Shen Rongsheng’s side and whispered urgently: “Master, the Madam is here.”

Shen Rongsheng’s face stiffened. He forgot about seeing Zhang Yuanheng off and let his own attendant escort the guest, while he turned and doubled back hastily.

Zhang Yuanheng had been about to politely decline a personal escort, but seeing Shen Rongsheng’s urgent expression and the faint crease between his brows, he knew it would be unkind to add to his troubles and took his leave with his attendants.

Shen Rongsheng had barely reached the study door when Madam Wen appeared with a retinue of matrons: “I get back and there’s no sign of you anywhere. Your elder brother has returned — go to his quarters and at least put on a show of helping him deal with this matter. Keep up appearances.”

chapters.title: Blocked by Song Zhang
chapters.content:
Shen Rongsheng pinched the bridge of his nose. He gave Madam Wen a look: “Xu’er was never the reliable sort. Song Zhang arresting someone doesn’t necessarily mean there’s no evidence. This has nothing to do with us — why should we involve ourselves?”

“Even if someone from the Duke’s household comes looking for me, I won’t see them.”

He turned his sleeve to leave — but before he could take a single step, Madam Wen grabbed him by the ear: “No matter what else Xu’er may be, he is still Zhi’an’s younger brother. The man wrote asking for help. Are you really going to do nothing? He will be Zhao-zhao’s brother-in-law — with that connection in place, how can you ignore it?”

Shen Rongsheng winced from the pain, but under Madam Wen’s pressure he could only sigh and agree: “Fine, fine, I’ll go speak to Elder Brother. Whether it does any good or not — don’t blame me.”

“When Song Zhang sets his mind to something, ordinary people cannot pull him back.”

Madam Wen released him and smiled: “Good. Go — then I can send a reply.”

Shen Rongsheng had no choice but to go.

Meanwhile, Shen Weici was making her way back with the calligraphy copy Zhang Yuanheng had given her tucked in her arms. The sky was only just beginning to darken — still light enough to see the path clearly, and the lack of a lantern was no great inconvenience.

Her courtyard in the Rear West Wing was a quiet, out-of-the-way place, adjoining the back garden, and few people passed through. So she slowed her steps a little and took in the scenery of the estate at her leisure.

Yue Deng walked at her side, beaming: “That Master Zhang is truly like jade come to life, young miss. The Second Master found you a wonderful match.”

Shen Weici could not help but lower her head and look at the calligraphy copy in her hands. The volume was in excellent condition. Even for a rare surviving edition over a century old, the paper was still nearly as fresh as new — a testament to how dearly its previous owner had prized it.

She thought of the warm, steady look in Zhang Yuanheng’s eyes — the only pair of eyes in the capital that had looked at her with genuine goodwill.

Inside her father’s study he had also been wonderfully attentive: he had poured tea for her himself, ground ink for her himself. He had been so quietly considerate that Shen Weici had not even anticipated it.

She rubbed the pages softly with her fingertip, and a faint smile appeared at the corner of her lips.

She murmured: “Whether this comes to anything is still uncertain. Don’t mention it to anyone outside. We don’t want word getting out.”

Yue Deng laughed and clapped a hand over her mouth, nodding vigorously: “The young miss can count on me. I promise I won’t say a word.”

Shen Weici smiled — but in the next instant, the smile froze on her face. She had spotted Song Zhang coming down the path ahead, leading two large black dogs.

This path was the only route back to her courtyard; no other courtyard opened onto it. She had no idea why Song Zhang was passing through here, but her eyes fell on the black dogs standing nearly as tall as a man’s waist, and she took a step back.

Song Zhang noticed Shen Weici’s smile vanish the moment she saw him, and the memory of the laugh he had heard from her room the night before rose unbidden in his mind.

It had been fine and soft, like a feather tickling him — it had set something stirring in his chest that would not quite settle.

The sky was still dim just now, but he had quite distinctly seen her smile. And yet it had vanished in an instant, replaced by wary eyes that watched him.

He raised an eyebrow, led his dogs over, and came to stand before Shen Weici: “Is Third Miss Shen afraid of me?”

Song Zhang stepped so close that Shen Weici could catch the cool, faintly spiced scent on him — could feel the warmth radiating from his body.

She stepped back and looked up at Song Zhang’s face, half-lit in the half-dark: “The young master is imagining things.”

Song Zhang let out a scoffing laugh. Looking down, he noticed the volume she was clutching tightly, and then her wary, guarded eyes — an expression he found distinctly unsettling.

His dark gaze came to rest on her face: “If you’re not afraid of me, then why step back?”

Song Zhang was very tall. To speak with him, she had to tilt her head back; looking down, she could see no further than his chest.

The constant craning of her neck was tiring, and she had no desire to look at that arrogantly set face, so she said quietly: “Perhaps it is because the young master is standing too close.”

Song Zhang looked at the distance between them — still a full pace apart. Where was that close?

He gave a smile that didn’t reach his eyes and stepped forward until the toe of his shoe nearly touched hers, bending slightly toward her: “Now this is close. Would Third Miss Shen not agree?”

His hot breath swept across her face. The darkness around them was dense and heavy, and there was no one else nearby. If some passing maidservant caught sight of this scene and word got out, the reputation damaged would be hers.

Over these past few days she had also gathered some information about Song Zhang’s position in the household. Although he had come to the estate when his mother, the Commandery Princess Huimin, remarried the First Master, he still bore the surname Song — he was the sole heir of the Song Duke household, the heir apparent of that family, with no real connection to the Marquis household.

The two of them standing this close was genuinely improper.

Her expression tightened, and just as she was about to step back again, she realized that the wolfhound at Song Zhang’s side had somehow slipped around behind her without her noticing. Her retreating embroidered shoe came down on its paw, and the dog immediately bared its sharp teeth and lunged toward her as if to bite.

Shen Weici had always been terrified of dogs. She flinched and snatched her foot back, then looked up at Song Zhang’s face: “What is it that Young Master Song wants?”

Song Zhang found Shen Weici’s expression — no longer the calm, blank composure she usually wore — rather entertaining.

He even thought those eyes, glaring at him, were quite remarkably beautiful.

His gaze was languid and detached. He bent slightly toward her and, in the gathering dimness, studied the smooth paleness of her cheek and let his eyes drift to those cherry-red lips: “What does Third Miss Shen think I want?”

Those lips were truly small — like a single cherry, with a gentle fullness. Though he could not see her clearly in this light, he could have sworn they were the most vivid shade of red.

Shen Weici had not imagined Song Zhang would be so bold. His nose was nearly touching hers.

She could not understand what this man intended. Or perhaps he simply found her easy to push around.

The autumn evening darkened quickly, and the breath so close to her face made her heart flutter with a panicked feeling she could not quite name.

She tightened the fingers gripping the calligraphy copy, pushed down the strange, searing shame that felt like a slow humiliation, and clenched her jaw as she tried to slip past him to one side.

But the dog behind her seemed to understand its master’s unspoken wishes — whichever way she moved, it blocked her.

In the dim haze she caught a glimpse of the one who had arranged all of this: he was watching the whole spectacle as if it were a performance staged for his amusement, and she was a puppet in his palm, being observed with idle curiosity.

She bit her teeth together, then suddenly pushed Song Zhang aside with both hands and darted for the gap she had made.

But there came a fierce, sharp bark, and the dog seized the hem of her skirt in its jaws. She was moving too quickly, and the pull brought her crashing to the ground.

Yue Deng rushed forward to help her — but before she could take a single step, a sword appeared across her path. She stumbled back in fright, her face draining white, and turned to see a cold-faced, handsome young man staring at her just as coldly. The icy light in his eyes struck terror into her heart, and she cried out: “What are you trying to do?”

Minhe did not answer her. He only shot her one frigid look, his expression utterly merciless.

Song Zhang stood with his arms folded, watching Shen Weici bracing herself on the ground as she tried to rise, then crouched down before her: “Third Miss Shen had best not make any sudden moves. When you pushed me just now, in its eyes you became prey. If you struggle too hard, it will spring and snap your neck in an instant.”

Shen Weici froze, mid-attempt to rise. Her eyes slowly reddened — but the sky had grown dark enough that Song Zhang could not see the weakness on her face.

She blinked, fingertips scraping against the cold stone beneath her until they stung, and asked: “Why is Young Master Song doing this to me?”

chapters.title: How About Giving Me a Smile
chapters.content:
Song Zhang breathed in the fragrance that was barely an inch from him. He had been thinking about this scent for days — his mind had chased it during his daytime patrols of the Imperial Palace, and it had lingered when he lay down to sleep at night.

No other woman carried this scent. Only Shen Weici.

That faint, tenacious fragrance — like wild orchids growing on high mountain ridges, so light and airy it seemed to dissolve when you tried to catch it, yet impossible to forget.

He thought with uncharacteristic care about Shen Weici’s question: why was he doing this to her?

He could not arrive at a satisfying answer. He only knew he found her easy to approach — that he kept wanting to close the distance by a step or two, to find some pretext, to catch a glimpse of an expression he had not seen on her face before.

It was like slowly uncovering things about her he had not known — and that brought a kind of satisfaction no other thing could.

As though he were, by degrees, getting her under his control.

Song Zhang thought that sensation felt very good. At least, he had never felt anything quite like it before.

He made a vague sound, as though genuinely giving the question his careful consideration — yet his unrestrained gaze never left Shen Weici. It was a pity the sky had darkened, and though her pale, smooth complexion was still just visible, those eyes of hers, which always drew his own, had been swallowed by the shadows.

He tapped a finger idly on his knee and glanced down at her: “Now that you put it that way — I suppose I have been a little hard on you.”

“How about you give me a smile? Then I’ll let you go.”

Shen Weici was taken aback. In these circumstances, she could not possibly smile. She tried to pull the hem of her skirt free from the dog’s teeth, but she could not get it loose no matter what she did.

She did not want to go on tangled up with this man in such a demeaning situation any longer — and she especially did not want to flatter him with a smile, earning her own release by catering to his whims.

Seeing no response from Shen Weici, Song Zhang reached out and directly seized her by the chin, his face pressing in close: “It’s too dark for me to see. Smile now — let me look.”

He had her chin in his grip. Her body, braced against the ground, tilted toward him. His face was almost level with hers, their breaths mingling. She felt nothing but deep, scalding humiliation, and the wetness she had been holding back in her eyes could be contained no longer — it rolled down her cheek, silent and involuntary.

Song Zhang felt the warm dampness against his fingers and went still. He stared at Shen Weici’s eyes — she kept blinking, and through the shadows he could just make out the glimmer of tears at the corners, a faint rose-pink blush, not a sound escaping her. Yet the wetness against his fingertip was steady and unceasing.

He looked down at her parted lips, their faint warmth washing over him, that particular scent drifting out — and something shifted in his chest. His thumb moved, tracing the smooth line of her jaw, and after a long moment he finally released his grip.

He stood and pulled on the leash. The black dog obediently released the hem of her skirt and returned to stand at its master’s side.

Song Zhang’s lips pressed into a hard line. He glanced at Shen Weici still on the ground, lingered a moment — then looked away and turned, striding off into the dark.

In that fleeting instant, Song Zhang had felt an overwhelming urge to pull Shen Weici into his arms, to smooth away every trace of hurt she carried — and then to apologize to her with real contrition.

Even to coax her back to calm with humble words.

Song Zhang was furious at himself for the absurd impulse that had flashed through his mind. The only thing he could do was leave, before what was left of his self-control gave way entirely.

The sword that had barred Yue Deng’s path was withdrawn. She watched the avenging spirit who had stood in front of her finally walk away, then rushed over and knelt at Shen Weici’s side, helping her up: “Young miss, are you all right?”

Shen Weici groped along the ground until she found the calligraphy copy and pressed it tightly to herself. She took Yue Deng’s hand and forced herself upright.

The cool of deep autumn made the dampness at the corners of her eyes feel colder still. She said nothing and walked home, blinking steadily, fighting to push the last of the glimmer back where it had come from.

Two lanterns at the courtyard gate — their color faded — swayed faintly in the autumn wind with a kind of mournful restlessness. She stood at the gate and stared at them, at a loss.

The lanterns’ light fell across Shen Weici’s cheeks. Yue Deng turned to look at her, and saw that several strands of Shen Weici’s hair had come loose, her skirt was slightly rumpled, and there was dirt on it.

What made Yue Deng’s heart ache was the brightness she could see in her young miss’s eyes.

She had followed the young miss up mountain ridges in search of medicines and watched her roll down a slope without shedding a single tear.

Her own heart clenched in sympathy, and she was just opening her mouth to speak when she heard the young miss murmur: “I never want to be at the mercy of others again.”

Yue Deng ached for her. She linked her arm tightly through Shen Weici’s and whispered: “Master Zhang is certainly a good match for the young miss. Once you marry into his family, you’ll be the mistress of the house — you’ll never be beholden to anyone again.”

“Master Zhang will surely be good to you.”

Shen Weici looked silently at the ground: “I hope so.”

She left the rest of her words unspoken and walked into the courtyard.

The two maidservants guarding the courtyard gate saw that Shen Weici’s hair was in disarray and could not help following after her to ask: “What happened to the Third Miss?”

Yue Deng helped Shen Weici inside and said: “The young miss tripped on the way home in the dark. Go quickly and bring some hot water — the young miss’s hands are dirty.”

The two maidservants agreed and went off.

Inside the inner room, Yue Deng took Shen Weici’s hand and looked at it — and found the palm scraped raw in several places. Her heart broke as she hurried to wipe the dirt from those delicate white hands with a handkerchief, and she said, her voice sharp with indignation: “What is wrong with that Second Young Master Song? Why does he keep making trouble for the young miss?”

“Going around every day with that enormous dog — what if it actually bites someone one day?”

“Is there no one in this household who can manage him?”

“And that aide of his is frightening too — looks at you like a demon who’s owed money.”

Shen Weici looked at her palm quietly: “If there were someone who could manage him in this household, they would not have let him keep that dog in the first place.”

Yue Deng paused, then looked at Shen Weici with a puzzled expression: “Why is it that the Commandery Princess Huimin remarried the First Master, but there are no children in the First Branch — only Second Young Master Song? Where would the title go in the end?”

Shen Weici glanced at her: “You do pay attention to these things.”

The hot water arrived from outside just then. Yue Deng hurried to dampen a cloth and wiped Shen Weici’s hands with it, talking as she worked: “It’s not that I’m nosy — it’s just what I hear from the other maidservants.”

“Some say it will pass to the eldest son of the Third Branch. Others say that although Eldest Young Master Shen has an official rank, he lacks talent, and his maternal family is somewhat modest in standing, while Third Master is an idle man who drinks and wastes his days — the household couldn’t rest on his shoulders. Since the Emperor favors Second Young Master Song, perhaps he will allow Song Zhang to inherit the title.”

“Though that is a little hard to account for.”

“Anyway, the servants say all sorts of things.”

Shen Weici looked at Yue Deng: “Where are you hearing all this?”

Yue Deng said: “The servants talk when there’s nothing to do. I hear it all when I go to the kitchen for meals — maidservants from every branch are there, and they know everything.”

“And apparently Third Master has worn out his health yet still wants to take a concubine, so he went and bought some special medicines. But the medicines were fakes, and instead he ended up with diarrhea all night long. All the maidservants were laughing themselves senseless over it.”

Shen Weici said quietly to Yue Deng: “You can listen to all of this — but you must not join in the gossiping. We should keep a low profile in this household as much as possible, so as not to cause any mishaps.”

Yue Deng smiled: “You’ve said this several times already, miss. I remember.”

She cleaned Shen Weici’s hands and went for the medicine Shen Rongsheng had sent over to apply: “Thank goodness the Second Master sent you that salve. It cleared up the mark on your cheek overnight — your hand should heal just as fast.”

Shen Weici looked at the raw scrapes on her palm. The white, cool ointment spread across it brought a stinging, burning pain. The skin was red enough to make one wince.

She had always had a high tolerance for pain. Her other hand moved to her knee, still a dull ache beneath her fingers, and she coughed twice: “Winter is nearly here.”

Yue Deng, not looking up, replied: “I wonder if the snow is heavy in the capital. The young miss always hated snow.”

chapters.title: A Letter from Second Young Master Zhang
chapters.content:
Shen Weici hated the snow because it made people cold — and the cold made the cruelty of human nature impossible to conceal.

Ashamed that her mother had returned to the family home alone with a child, her grandmother had driven them out without a shred of mercy — only to come knocking, her uncle in tow, the moment word reached her that her mother was doing well.

They claimed the best rooms in the house, seized all the silver her father had left her mother, and installed Shen Weici and her mother in a damp western chamber.

The snow was bitterly cold, and there was no charcoal fire. She had pressed herself against the windowsill and stared at the unbroken white outside, listening to the coughing behind her from the bed where her mother lay, wondering how much longer before the snow would finally stop.

One winter passed into the next. One year into another.

Dressed in a single unlined white robe, she sat propped against the bed, frowning as she drank her medicine. Yue Deng’s voice murmured in her ear: “That Master Zhang today was truly a gentleman polished to jade — did you hear how he spoke, young miss? Unhurried and steady, with such a pleasant voice. And his eyes never wandered over the young miss the way those other men’s do.”

“And the way he dressed — none of those gaudy, flashy ornaments. Not even a jade pendant at his waist; just a flute tucked there instead. Clearly a man of refined taste, not the sort to behave rashly. The young miss marrying him would certainly be a life of harmony and mutual respect.”

Shen Weici listened to Yue Deng and could not help smiling: “Your mind has already gotten that far ahead.”

“But seeing him today — he does seem like a very fine young man.”

Yue Deng giggled and covered her mouth: “Does that mean the young miss has fallen for him?”

Shen Weici smiled a little: “Not quite. But he is warm and courteous, proper in every manner — one can see at a glance that he was raised with great care. A gentleman of that kind is rare.”

She put the empty bowl into Yue Deng’s hands and dabbed at the corner of her mouth with a handkerchief: “But let’s not speak of his affairs yet. We’ll wait and see what Father says next.”

Yue Deng took the bowl and made an affirmative sound, then went to slide a warming stone into the quilts: “Who knows how long this cold will last. I think the days are starting to feel like winter.”

“Is the young miss’s knee still hurting?”

It was still somewhat painful. When she touched it, everything felt cold, but the warming stone helped a great deal.

Shen Weici lay on her side with her hair unbound, the dark strands falling past her shoulder, leaving a small, smooth length of pale neck exposed.

She looked at Yue Deng and said softly: “You should sleep early too. You didn’t rest properly last night keeping me company — get to bed sooner tonight.”

Yue Deng hummed in agreement, pulled the bed curtains down around Shen Weici, and slipped out.

On the second afternoon, a young manservant she did not recognize came to the door delivering something. Shen Weici asked which part of the estate he served, and the boy smiled: “I serve at the front gate, miss. This was brought by someone from the Yiyong Earldom — they asked me to deliver it to Third Miss.”

Shen Weici heard ‘Earldom’ and looked at the small box the boy was holding out, with a letter resting on top of it. She took them both, then asked Yue Deng to give the boy a tip and see him out.

She carried the items to the desk and sat down, setting aside the box and taking the letter in hand, leaning back in her chair.

She recognized the handwriting on the envelope — it was Zhang Yuanheng’s.

She looked at the seal of the Earl’s estate pressed in wax and felt, for a moment, a slight dizziness of disbelief.

With unhurried fingers she opened the letter. A faint smell of ink drifted up. She unfolded the paper to find neat, practiced characters.

She lowered her lashes and read carefully.

Yue Deng came back in from seeing the boy out, and no sooner had she lifted the curtain than she saw the young miss sitting at the window, bathed in the mellow afternoon light — peaceful and soft, the silver hairpin glinting in her dark hair. Yue Deng instinctively lightened her footsteps.

She stood by the desk and quietly poured a cup of tea, then waited until Shen Weici had finished reading before offering it to her and asking: “Young miss, is it a letter from Master Zhang?”

Shen Weici nodded. She held the letter and stared at it for a moment, then folded it neatly and set it on the table, reaching for the teacup in Yue Deng’s hand.

Yue Deng glanced at the letter on the table, curious: “What did Master Zhang write?”

Shen Weici lowered her gaze over the rim of the teacup. Steam rose and warmed her face. She narrowed her eyes against it, and when she looked up again, there was a gentle smile on her face.

“Master Zhang says he heard yesterday that my health is delicate, and he noticed me coughing. It concerned him. He has sent a box of Crimson Gauze Pills to strengthen my constitution — he says they invigorate the vital energy, replenish the blood, and are also beneficial for a cough.”

Yue Deng exclaimed with delighted surprise: “I never imagined Master Zhang would be so thoughtful — this means he truly has the young miss in his heart.”

She reached for the box on the table and held it out: “Young miss, shall we open it and have a look?”

Shen Weici looked at the beautifully carved wooden box and nodded.

Yue Deng eagerly lifted the lid. A light, unusual fragrance drifted out, and she saw that the interior was divided into ten small compartments, each holding a single pill — two layers in all, roughly twenty small pills, each no larger than a fingernail.

Yue Deng held one up to her eye: “This looks like it ought to be extremely precious.”

“I’ve heard that many noble young ladies in the capital take all sorts of fragrant-body pills, beauty-cultivating pills, and the like. Perhaps this supplement will actually do some good.”

Shen Weici leaned against the armrest of her daybed: “Set it aside for now.”

Yue Deng looked at her, puzzled: “But they’re meant to be taken. What’s the point of just setting them aside?”

“After all, they are Master Zhang’s genuine good intentions. Doesn’t this mean he has the young miss in his heart? Isn’t that a good thing?”

Shen Weici looked at Yue Deng and smiled softly: “I am, of course, happy to know Master Zhang’s intentions.”

“But whether this marriage can come to anything, I still don’t know. I don’t know whether he truly intends to propose. If he has no such intention — if he only sent these things out of a momentary fondness after meeting me just once — I would rather not keep them. I would return them to him later, to leave no room for anyone to speak ill.”

“But if he truly has feelings for me and is willing to come and propose, then naturally I would be happy to accept anything he gives.”

Yue Deng sat beside Shen Weici and thought for a moment: “The way Master Zhang concerns himself with the young miss’s health — surely he must have that intention?”

Shen Weici gazed down at the tea leaves floating in her cup. Her cold fingers clung to the warmth of the celadon cup. She said quietly: “Who can say for certain.”

“He is young, accomplished, and in the Emperor’s inner circle — his future is limitless. Perhaps he is also looking for a wife who can offer him some advantage in his career.”

“If he were to marry me, I could bring him nothing. All I could offer is to free him from worry at home, to manage the household carefully on his behalf. Beyond that, I have nothing more to give.”

Yue Deng started: “I don’t think Master Zhang seems like that kind of calculating person.”

Shen Weici smiled: “Nothing in this world is ever certain. Let’s wait and see a little longer.”

Yue Deng nodded obediently, closed the lid of the wooden box, put it away in the cabinet, then turned to find the young miss spreading paper on the desk, as though to write.

She hurried over to grind the ink: “What is the young miss going to write?”

Shen Weici looked out the window at the light, which was bright enough to be slightly harsh. The bare flower branches trembled lightly in the wind. She said softly: “He wrote to ask after my health — naturally I must write back to him.”

As she spoke she dipped the brush in ink and began. She deliberately used the brushwork technique Zhang Yuanheng had shown her yesterday. She had only learned a fraction of it, but even that showed she had not set his calligraphy copy aside — it was her way of acknowledging his thoughtfulness.

chapters.title: The Emperor Arranges a Marriage for Song Zhang
chapters.content:
The morning after she sent her letter out, Shen Weici had barely returned from Madam Wen’s and finished breakfast when the young manservant appeared again to deliver another letter.

Yue Deng gave him the same small tip and, smiling, saw him out.

Shen Weici rinsed her mouth and carried the letter to the inner room. She settled back into her chair and read.

The familiar seal on the envelope brought a small smile to her eyes.

This time the letter was a full two pages longer than the previous one. The opening, as before, asked after her health, the words warm and attentive — yet measured, never overstepping propriety, so that one did not feel the concern was excessive.

After that, he noted where the brushwork in her letter had been slightly off and wrote out several example characters to show her, patiently explaining each one.

At the very end came another word of concern: winter was nearly here, the wind was cold, and he urged her to drink more cinnamon-bark tea to ward off the chill.

The autumn breeze outside drifted across Shen Weici’s cheeks, yet she felt a warm current move through her, a small tenderness touching the tip of her heart.

It had been a long time since anyone had cared for her like this.

Yue Deng came back and saw the smile in Shen Weici’s eyes. She could not help smiling too: “What’s the young miss smiling about?”

Shen Weici looked at Yue Deng: “I didn’t expect Master Zhang to write back so quickly.”

Yue Deng said: “That just means Master Zhang is thinking of the young miss.”

“Does the young miss think of Master Zhang?”

Shen Weici paused, then shook her head slowly: “I’m not sure.”

“But receiving his letter — seeing how careful and considerate it is, how warm and proper — it makes me glad.”

Yue Deng giggled: “Then that proves the young miss has feelings for him too.”

Shen Weici looked down at the letter in her hands. The words, line by line, were before her eyes. She said quietly: “But I don’t want to fix all my hope on one person.”

“That way my heart won’t be left with nothing when it falls.”

Yue Deng thought for a moment: “Why not ask the Second Master — does Master Zhang actually intend to marry the young miss or not?”

“The way I see it, Master Zhang writing so frequently and eagerly — he surely wants to marry you.”

Shen Weici set down the letter and rose to go to the low table and unpick the stitches on a few more garments. She said quietly: “These past couple of days I’ve noticed Father has been rather busy. He wasn’t even there when I went to pay my respects this morning. We’ve only just met a few days ago — it wouldn’t do for me to go and ask already.”

“There’s no great rush. We’ll discuss it later.”

Yue Deng helped her thread the needle: “Will the young miss not write back to Master Zhang then?”

Shen Weici thought it over: “I’ll wait two days before writing back. There’s no urgency.”

Yue Deng nodded: “That’s true.”

Meanwhile, in the Imperial Palace, Song Zhang was accompanying the Emperor through a stroll in the Imperial Gardens. The Emperor looked at Song Zhang, his expression grave: “I hear you’ve had Xu’er from the Yong’an Marquis household arrested and sent to the Office of Pending Punishment?”

Song Zhang only smiled: “His Majesty is well-informed.”

The Emperor let out a sardonic chuckle: “Consort Xu came to me in tears. How could I not know?”

He stopped walking and turned to Song Zhang: “Tell me — Xu’er is nothing but a wastrel second son. Why did you bother arresting him?”

Song Zhang stood before the Emperor and made a proper bow: “With no Crown Prince yet named, Xu’er has been spreading word outside that Your Majesty intends to elevate the Fourth Prince — the son of Noble Consort Zhang — to heir apparent, stirring up suspicion and rivalry among the princes. Would Your Majesty say he deserved to be arrested?”

The Emperor heard this and sighed: “You are not wrong. My continued delay in naming an heir has become a source of instability. I cannot put it off any longer.”

He looked at Song Zhang: “Whom do you think I should name as Crown Prince?”

Song Zhang immediately bowed his head: “Your servant exists only to ensure Your Majesty’s safety and to assist with matters that trouble you. The question of the Crown Prince is not one Your servant should presume to comment upon.”

The Emperor studied Song Zhang for a moment, then smiled: “You’re rather formal and reverent before me these days. When you were small, you used to sit on your maternal grandmother’s lap and ask to play with my imperial seal.”

“I said you could have it if you wanted it. You jumped straight down from your grandmother’s arms and said yes, just like that. Every palace maid and eunuch within sight dropped to their knees. Even your grandmother was so frightened she held you down and knelt — but you stood there before me, bold as you please, as if you weren’t quite satisfied with how things had turned out.”

“You certainly don’t have that kind of audacity anymore.”

Song Zhang finally raised his head and gave a rueful smile: “I was too young to know better. And Your Majesty indulged me terribly.”

The Emperor smiled: “Song Zhang — you know full well that I have always indulged you because I trust you.”

“You are the man closest to my side. With you near me, I am at ease.”

“Now my sons are all stirring and jostling for position. I need you to keep a close watch on the Fourth Prince and the Second Prince. For the Third Prince, out with the frontier garrison, send men you trust to keep an eye on things.”

“A report every seven days — whatever they do, I want to know.”

Song Zhang looked pained: “That many people to watch — does Your Majesty think I can manage it all?”

The Emperor gave him a sideways look: “Why else would I give you command of the Left and Right Guards and the Jinwu Guards? So you could breed reliable men — with that many pairs of eyes at your disposal, you still can’t keep watch?”

He clapped Song Zhang on the shoulder: “Don’t worry — I will reward you generously in due course. The rank of General of the Grand Armies will be yours, and the prestige will suit you well.”

“Furthermore, my most beloved daughter, Princess Zhao-rou, I intend to give to you in marriage. Be at ease — I will not shortchange you.”

Song Zhang was taken aback. Seeing from the Emperor’s expression that this was no idle jest, he looked at him and said: “Your servant is not yet inclined to discuss marriage. There are still pleasures outside that your servant has not fully enjoyed — once married, I fear I would no longer feel free to enjoy them.”

The Emperor burst out laughing: “Honest, at least.”

“But your maternal grandmother came to me just the other day to speak about your marriage — asking me to select a fine match for you, someone truly outstanding in every regard.”

“And the Song Dukedom has only you, a single heir. If you keep putting marriage off, where are your descendants to come from?”

“Old Duke Song is still out there guarding the frontier at his age — I feel sorry for him. Your marriage cannot be delayed any further. I’ll give you six months to think it over. If you haven’t chosen someone by then, I will make the choice for you.”

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor with a suffering expression: “May your servant make the choice himself?”

The Emperor’s face turned severe: “Naturally I cannot indulge you that far. The candidate must meet with my approval, your maternal grandmother’s approval, and Duke Song’s approval first. Family background and character must both be of the first order — only then would she be worthy.”

Song Zhang heard this and gave a pained smile: “Those women are always putting on such a performance in front of others. How tedious.”

The Emperor blew out his beard in a huff: “Now you’re being picky? Can any ordinary woman compare to a family of good standing?”

“Besides, you take a wife and then keep a few favorites on the side if you like — no one expects you to spend your whole life devoted to a single woman.”

Song Zhang asked the Emperor quite earnestly: “Even if I marry the Princess, I can still take concubines?”

The Emperor gave him a look: “Just don’t go too far. If there’s a scene, I’ll be the one with the headache.”

Song Zhang only smiled.

He accompanied the Emperor back to the Hall of Diligent Governance, and no sooner had he stepped back out than he turned and found Fifth Princess Zhao-rou hiding behind one of the crimson pillars, peeking at him. He raised an eyebrow and moved to go — but the Fifth Princess darted out and blocked his path, holding out her hand: “Song Zhang, I want you to go catch me a bird.”

Song Zhang looked down at the Fifth Princess looking up at him, then raised two fingers to his lips and blew a short whistle. In no time at all, a golden eagle landed on his forearm. He held it out toward the Fifth Princess: “Would you like this?”

Princess Zhao-rou was startled backward several steps by the massive, beating wings, then pointed at Song Zhang, trembling with fury: “Song Zhang, you are bullying me!”

Song Zhang gave her a bored look, then turned his back on her without further ceremony and walked away, the golden eagle perched on his arm.

chapters.title: Zhang Yuanheng Again
chapters.content:
The next few days passed peacefully for Shen Weici. During the day she let out and adjusted garments; in the evenings she practiced calligraphy.

When she went to pay her respects to Madam Wen, Madam Wen gave her no particular trouble — said a few words and sent her back. Even Shen Zhaozhao had not come looking for her.

Shen Weici felt slightly unsettled by the quiet. It was not as though the cold look in Madam Wen’s eyes or the contempt in Shen Zhaozhao’s had been feigned when she first came to the estate. This unnatural calm made her vaguely uneasy.

Yue Deng laughed at her: “Young miss, you’re thinking too much. The Second Master must have given Second Young Miss a talking-to after the last incident. They certainly don’t want the other branches gossiping.”

“Besides, you are perfectly polite and never say more than you should when you go. What could she possibly do — grab you and bite you?”

Shen Weici smiled a little and bent her attention back to the needlework in her hand.

That afternoon, Father’s personal attendant came with an invitation to visit the study.

Shen Weici knew the way well by now. She tidied her needlework and left with Yue Deng.

Yue Deng crept close and whispered: “Why is the Master asking the young miss to the study again? Could it be news about Master Zhang? Is he coming to propose?”

Shen Weici smiled: “It probably won’t be that soon.”

When she stepped into the main hall of Tingzhu Pavilion, she found Zhang Yuanheng already there, seated across from her father in conversation. She had barely looked up when Zhang Yuanheng stopped speaking and his gaze turned toward her.

He wore a plain sky-blue round-collar robe, a jade pendant at his waist, and a faint smile in his eyes as he looked at her — warm and gentle as sunlight.

Shen Weici’s heart skipped a beat. She lowered her gaze and paid her respects to her father.

Shen Rongsheng smiled at her entrance: “Come, find a seat — I was just telling Zhang Er-lang about you.”

“Zhang Er-lang says your calligraphy has improved. He came today specifically to teach you. Have you thanked him yet?”

Shen Weici had only just settled into a seat across the room when she heard her father’s words. She looked up at Zhang Yuanheng and offered a half-bow: “Thank you, Master Zhang.”

Zhang Yuanheng could not help his gaze from resting on Shen Weici across the room. She wore a deep-blue robe embroidered with intricate red peonies on a wide-sleeved background — the open sleeves half-concealing her jade fingers, making what was left of them appear even more slender, each one perfectly shaped.

She wore no powder or rouge, in contrast to the somewhat bright dress. Her hair was without ornament, her skin snowwhite, her lips red, her eyes dark as lacquer — like white snow with red plums: coolly vivid.

He felt a little dazed simply looking at her. He thought of the letter she had sent back — her small, neat, measured characters, somehow a little like her nature: quiet and still, yet in a way that put people at ease without making them feel constrained. Something warm stirred in his chest.

He stood and returned the bow: “Third Miss Shen need not thank me — rather, it is I who have been presumptuous in coming. Please do not hold it against me.”

Shen Weici smiled: “In fact I was looking for an opportunity to ask for instruction.”

That one smile made Zhang Yuanheng stare for a moment. He had thought her a little on the cool side last time — yet now he found himself thinking that her warmth was equally irresistible.

Shen Rongsheng had always been hoping to bring this match about. Seeing Zhang Yuanheng’s reaction, he was now almost certain — and smiled to himself: “Then let’s go to the study.”

Shen Rongsheng did not leave. Since the match had not yet been formally agreed upon, it would not do for Zhang Yuanheng and Shen Weici to be left alone together — that could only invite talk.

He settled back in the great armchair, unhurriedly drinking tea and reading, and left Shen Weici and Zhang Yuanheng standing at the desk to write.

Zhang Yuanheng had placed second in the Imperial Examination. His calligraphy was excellent, his poetry and prose even more so. He was regarded as one of the capital’s more accomplished young scholars. It was precisely his friendship with Zhang Yuanheng’s father that had made him think of this match in the first place.

He had only intended to test the waters — he had not expected this to have any real chance of coming together. Now he was more than pleased.

Meanwhile, Shen Weici’s wide sleeve swept across the desk. Zhang Yuanheng leaned over to look at her brushwork and offered a word of guidance here and there, though his hand remained perfectly proper — he never touched her, pointing only to the level of suggestion.

Yet in the places Shen Weici could not see, Zhang Yuanheng could not help stealing glances at her from the corner of his eye — at her soft, graceful profile, the focused and serious expression she wore, and that single bright beauty mark, all of which made him lose himself.

She had none of the exaggerated, deliberate shyness he had seen in other women, nor the forthright ease of still others. She was quietly, evenly warm — not coy, not bold — and it left him in a state he could not quite name, unsettled in the best possible way.

Since those last two days without a letter from her, he had barely been able to eat or sleep — every time he closed his eyes, he saw the curve of her downcast gaze.

And so, the moment his duty shift ended, he had come here.

He had told himself he only wanted to see her once — to steady that restless, ambiguous feeling in his chest.

Or perhaps he wanted to know what she thought of him.

Shen Weici finished a line and waited, but the person beside her had gone quiet for some time. She turned her head — and met Zhang Yuanheng’s eyes, fixed on her with a slightly dazed expression. She blinked and asked softly: “Master Zhang, how does what I’ve written look now?”

Zhang Yuanheng was, for once, briefly flustered. He quickly lowered his gaze to the paper on the desk.

The characters already had a good deal of feeling and ease to them. He had only shown her twice.

He said quietly: “Third Miss Shen is truly gifted. Before long you will be surpassing me.”

Shen Weici let out a light laugh: “I have only learned the surface. I am still far behind Master Zhang.”

“But practicing an hour every evening has made a difference.”

Zhang Yuanheng heard that laugh and could not keep himself from looking at her again. Her eyes shimmered with warmth, her brows curved gently, and his heart gave an involuntary small leap. He found himself smiling too.

He asked quietly: “I didn’t hear you cough just now — has your health improved these past few days?”

Shen Weici smiled: “I took your advice and tried boiling cinnamon bark in tea. It seems to have helped.”

Zhang Yuanheng said: “I can see your constitution is somewhat delicate. One of these days I’ll send along a few restorative prescriptions — my mother takes them as well. Perhaps they may be of some use.”

Shen Weici pressed her lips together and smiled: “You should not trouble yourself or go to any expense, Master Zhang. The household has its own prescriptions, and I am not so very unwell.”

Zhang Yuanheng paused, then let out a quiet, rueful laugh: “It is only my heartfelt wish.”

Shen Weici saw the look on his face and felt a flutter inside her — but in the end she said nothing.

As usual, Zhang Yuanheng took his leave as the sky began to darken. Shen Rongsheng specifically asked Shen Weici to see him to the gate while he remained behind — giving the two of them a moment to exchange a few words alone.

Shen Weici walked with Zhang Yuanheng to the covered corridor. A silence stretched between them as they made their way to the courtyard gate, where Zhang Yuanheng suddenly stopped. In the cold breeze, he looked at Shen Weici and said quietly: “I came without much notice today. Does Third Miss Shen feel I was too presumptuous?”

Shen Weici shook her head: “That Master Zhang came out of his busy days to teach me calligraphy — how could I think that presumptuous?”

Zhang Yuanheng looked steadily at Shen Weici’s eyes and said what was in his heart: “When I hadn’t received a reply letter from Third Miss Shen these past two days, I thought perhaps she found me too forward and had grown displeased with me.”

“I told myself to hold back — but I was too unsettled inside. I needed to see you once before I could be at ease.”

Taking advantage of the dimming sky, Zhang Yuanheng leaned ever so slightly in Shen Weici’s direction. His throat moved, and he asked the question that had been tormenting him: “I wonder — what impression do I make on Third Miss Shen?”

chapters.title: Whether Third Miss Shen Is Willing
chapters.content:
Shen Weici had not expected Zhang Yuanheng to ask her something so direct and unguarded.

She was, in truth, pleased with him — a young man of talent, from a respectable and scholarly family, the son of an Earldom, well-mannered and considerate toward her. From the very beginning she had wanted to make a good impression on him.

But if he was serious, he would come to propose. Propriety and the formal match were matters between parents. Why, then, would he ask for her own thoughts?

These words made Shen Weici’s regard for Zhang Yuanheng deepen.

She had only met him twice, yet she felt he deserved the name of a truly refined gentleman.

She had seen the slight daze in his eyes when he looked at her — perhaps he truly had some feeling for her.

The dry leaves at her feet stirred faintly with the breeze. She caught the faint smell of ink on him and opened her mouth: “Master Zhang is accomplished in both appearance and manner, warm and courteous — my impression is entirely favorable.”

Zhang Yuanheng felt the anxious weight in his chest ease at those words, and he made his promise: “Though you and I have met only twice, I have already made my decision. Once my mother returns from the countryside where she is tending to my grandmother’s illness, I will ask her to come and formally propose.”

“Is Third Miss Shen willing?”

Shen Weici was briefly startled, then looked up — and found Zhang Yuanheng’s gaze entirely serious.

Those eyes did not look as though they were dissembling. She answered him honestly: “My mother is gone. And my mother was no great family daughter — only an ordinary woman. I myself am not a favored daughter of this household; I am concubine-born, and my dowry will not be considerable.”

“I am naturally willing to marry Master Zhang. Only I ask that you think it over carefully. If, in the end, Master Zhang decides not to come with a proposal, I will hold no grudge.”

Zhang Yuanheng was about to speak when the figure before him stopped him: “Nor need Master Zhang rush to answer me now. Go home and think it through.”

As she said this, Shen Weici offered him a half-bow: “For now, let us part here.”

She raised her gaze halfway to meet his: “A matter of such importance — please also consult your family first, Master Zhang. If they are reluctant, I ask that you consider everything carefully.”

With that, Shen Weici lowered her eyes and turned, walking away with Yue Deng.

Zhang Yuanheng remained where he was, watching Shen Weici’s retreating figure — slender and graceful, her dark hair like a river down her back, those peach-blossom eyes that had looked at him leaving his mind a blank.

She had said she was not favored in her father’s household. She had asked him to go home and think it through carefully.

It was a slightly cool and distant thing to say. Yet somehow those words made the warmth in Zhang Yuanheng’s chest grow more intense.

They only made him want more to guard her and shield her from harm.

He stood there for a long time, until that last glimpse of her figure had faded entirely, before he finally turned to leave.

He had almost reached the gate when he came face to face with Song Zhang, who had just dismounted from his horse. He hurried forward to greet him with a bow: “General Song.”

Zhang Yuanheng spent a great deal of time in the Emperor’s presence recording events of significance. Song Zhang was also a constant companion at the Emperor’s side. Both had grown up in the capital, and they were at least nodding acquaintances.

Song Zhang and Zhang Yuanheng were not particularly close, but they were on civil terms. He dismounted with a slight nod and asked offhandedly: “What brings you here?”

Zhang Yuanheng smiled: “I came to discuss calligraphy with Minister Shen of the Second Branch.”

Song Zhang nodded. The Yiyong Earldom and the Marquis household had a degree of acquaintance. He asked nothing further, they exchanged a few pleasantries, and parted ways.

Back in her courtyard, Shen Weici sat down under the lamp and spread her palm open, studying the scabs forming over the scrapes. They were still faintly itchy.

The weather was very cold by now. No charcoal fire burned in the room. She brought her fingers close to the candle flame, borrowing a little of its warmth.

Yue Deng, who could not bear waiting any longer, sat beside Shen Weici and asked: “Master Zhang all but said outright that he’s coming to propose — why did the young miss say all that?”

“If a match like Master Zhang were to slip away, where else would the young miss ever find someone like him?”

“What if the Second Master decides not to bother searching carefully again for the young miss?”

Shen Weici rested her fingers against the warmth of the teacup, cradling it as she leaned back against the chair. The warm amber candlelight fell across her face, bringing out the soft curves of her features.

Her amber-colored eyes shone brighter in the lamplight, lashes long and catching the warmth: “If I had said nothing now, and it turned out that Master Zhang had come only because of the Marquis household, what would I have done then? A marriage made in unhappiness breeds resentment over the years — would that make for a good life?”

“I said those things in advance so he would go home and think it through carefully, and also explain things plainly to his family. Otherwise a marriage made on a moment’s liking alone — perhaps it might last three or five years — but as time passes, seeing his colleagues’ situations in comparison, how could grievances not eventually arise?”

“I don’t want to live that kind of life. Even if I were to miss this opportunity — even if I only married a commoner — as long as husband and wife are of one heart, and can face whatever comes together, without all that scheming and calculation, life would still be livable.”

“And I would have a place of my own.”

Yue Deng pouted: “But who doesn’t want to marry into a good family? The noble young ladies of the capital all aim for the highest matches they can get.”

“Once you’ve married in, what does it matter what anyone says? So long as the young miss does nothing wrong and manages her own affairs well, that’s all that’s needed.”

“And when children come in time — even if a husband isn’t ideal, at least there’s someone to depend on, isn’t there?”

Shen Weici leaned back with a small sigh: “Perhaps I’m only hoping for something more reliable and stable.”

In the days that followed, Zhang Yuanheng sent no more letters. But winter set in, and the weather turned cold, and a light, drizzling rain began to fall.

In the mid-afternoon, a young maidservant came to say that the Old Madam had decided that now the weather was cold, she would hold a gathering in the Rosy Pavilion in the garden, to roast meat and drink tea. She invited all the young ladies of the household to come and be merry.

The girl’s face was all smiles, her eyes bright and excited — it was clear she too wanted to go.

Shen Weici was not one to go out much. Unlike the other courtyard ladies who visited one another and walked together in the garden, she rarely left her rooms except to pay her respects to Madam Wen. But she could see that the maidservant had been cooped up with her and was more than a little restless, so she agreed to go.

She brought Yue Deng and Hexi along, and set out under a green oilpaper umbrella. Raindrops drummed down onto it in a light scatter, splashing into puddles at her feet and lightly wetting the toes of her embroidered shoes.

The garden was vast — Taihu stones and flowering trees layered and interlocked at every turn, a stream threading its way through. The carp inside had retreated to shelter beneath the garden rockery.

Shen Yanli, seated sideways on the railing, spotted Shen Weici’s figure approaching from a distance with her umbrella and turned back to say to Song Zhang, who was sitting at his side: “I didn’t expect you’d actually remember that Third Younger Sister wasn’t there. Even I forgot.”

Song Zhang said nothing. His deep, dark gaze rested on the figure who had just stepped up onto the arching stone bridge — the rain muting the colors of her dress, flickering and indistinct.

Shen Siwen looked at Song Zhang and, seeing he made no reply, thought better of pressing the matter. But it was odd to him — this was a man who never came to these sorts of gatherings. He had only said a word in passing, and somehow Song Zhang had actually come.

And having come, he had done nothing — neither eaten nor talked — sitting there with that glacial, forbidding air that made Shen Siwen feel inexplicably inhibited in his own conversation.

He had barely spent time in the estate at all before. Why was he suddenly so at leisure?

Shen Weici meanwhile held her skirt hem with two fingers and picked her way along the path until she finally arrived.

The pavilion had three stories. The Old Madam and the others were on the third floor. A few maidservants guarded the lower floors. Seeing another guest arrive, one of them came forward to take the cloak she had unfastened and carry it to the side room to dry on a rack.

Shen Weici turned and looked at the rippling surface of the green pool behind her, then lowered her gaze and climbed the stairs.

The lively sounds of laughter could already be heard from below; reaching the top, they were louder still. Warmth swept over her, and the joking and chatter rang out one after another.

Shen Weici paused at the top of the stairs. No one seemed to have noticed her. She saw that everyone was gathered around the roasting brazier. The Old Madam sat at the head, surrounded by the unmarried young ladies of the household, talking and laughing. To one side stood Shen Yanli and the Fourth Young Master Shen Siwen, both smiling and joining in.

Shen Weici stood at the corner of the stairwell, listening to the sounds of merriment. She suddenly felt like an outsider.

The rack above was already laden with several roasted pieces of meat. Everyone was all present; she was the last to arrive. It was obvious she had been remembered partway through and sent for.

The matron standing at the Old Madam’s side spotted Shen Weici and called out warmly: “Third Miss is here — the Old Madam has been asking about you.”

That one remark drew all eyes toward her. Shen Zhaozhao looked at Shen Weici wearing those flashy colors so well and could not suppress a flicker of jealousy, responding with a cold, dismissive sound.

Feeling all those gazes on her, Shen Weici pressed down the thoughts that stirred in her chest, put on a smile, and walked over to pay her respects to the Old Madam.

From the corner of her eye she caught sight of Song Zhang too, and looked away.

Shen Old Madam smiled and patted the space beside her: “Come sit with me, child.” Then, to Shen Yanli: “Your Third Sister is here — pour her a small cup of warm wine to take the chill off.”

chapters.title: The Flying Flower Poetry Game
chapters.content:
Shen Weici settled beside the Old Madam. The chill she had carried in from outside was quickly warmed away by the press of people around her.

She looked at the small pink porcelain cup Shen Yanli was smiling and holding out, and heard him say: “Third Younger Sister, this is cherry wine — there is rose honey in it as well. It is wonderfully sweet and fragrant, and I promise you will want more once you’ve tasted it.”

Shen Weici had never drunk wine before. She was on the verge of declining, but seeing that no one else had said anything, and that Shen Yanli was already holding the cup right up to her, and that it was the Old Madam who had asked — she could not well refuse and spoil the mood. She took it with a small smile.

She glanced at the cup and took a delicate sip — faintly sour, faintly sweet, with the barest suggestion of wine. Not particularly unpleasant, but not quite pleasant either.

It was her first time drinking, and she took only one sip. Shen Yanli noticed and immediately made a show of urging her on: “Who drinks wine one sip at a time? Even Fifth Younger Sister can knock back three cups in a row — how can Third Younger Sister not finish at least one cup?”

Shen Zhaozhao’s lip curled coldly: “I’d say she’s never had anything good and wouldn’t know how to appreciate it if you gave it to her.”

The Old Madam said to Shen Weici at her side: “Fruit wine doesn’t make you drunk. Drinking it all in one go is the only way to warm yourself up properly.”

With the Old Madam saying so, Shen Weici had little choice but to drink the whole cup.

The empty cup was quickly refilled by Shen Yanli, though to his credit he did not press her further. He and Shen Siwen busied themselves with slicing and roasting meat.

Once the meat was roasted and salt sprinkled over it, the savory aroma rose around them. Outside, cold rain fell on and on. Inside, they circled the brazier eating meat and drinking wine, watching the rain-drenched view — it was its own kind of pleasure.

Shen Weici was given a pair of silver chopsticks and picked up a small piece to try.

The talk continued and the gathering stayed lively, but Shen Weici could not join in. She took a couple of bites and sat quietly listening.

They spoke mostly of happenings in the capital — which two families had become engaged, what incident had occurred in someone else’s household. In the capital, everyone’s affairs were intertwined; the great families were mostly acquainted with one another, and even those they didn’t know well could supply some interesting piece of gossip.

She was listening quietly to all of it when the Old Madam suddenly took her hand and said: “On ordinary days, go out and chat with people. Don’t sit alone in your courtyard — it must be dull, mustn’t it?”

“Walk around the garden more, and spend time with the young ladies here — get to know one another better.”

Shen Weici nodded with docile compliance: “Please don’t worry on my account, Old Madam. I’ll remember.”

Shen Old Madam studied Shen Weici’s face carefully. Among all the young ladies of the household, she was undeniably the most beautiful, and her bearing and conduct were equally fine — gentle and composed, without any of the recklessness or wild swings of mood that youth sometimes brought. A temperament like that was rare.

A faint pang of guilt toward the girl stirred in the Old Madam’s heart.

She also noticed that Shen Weici’s hair still had not a single ornament — no eardrops, no bracelets — and that she relied on nothing but her face to stand out. She asked: “I see you have no jewelry on you at all. Is it that you haven’t any, or you simply don’t wear it?”

At those words, Shen Weici felt a sharp look lance toward her from somewhere nearby. Her expression did not change. She looked at the Old Madam and said quietly: “My stepmother arranged a great many pieces of jewelry for me, and Second Elder Sister gave me a whole boxful as well. But I was never in the habit of wearing jewelry, and I worry about losing pieces that are too valuable — I thought I would save them for more important occasions.”

Shen Zhaozhao heard this and gave a thin, contemptuous laugh: “Giving nice things to her really is a waste.”

Shen Old Madam frowned at Shen Zhaozhao: “Hold your tongue. You are sisters — you should get along.”

Shen Zhaozhao, who had never been addressed so sternly by her grandmother, was startled into silence.

Shen Old Madam turned back to Shen Weici: “It won’t do to go without jewelry. At the very least you are now a young lady of the Marquis household. If people from outside were to see you, they might think the household has given you nothing.”

Shen Weici looked up at the Old Madam: “Then I will do as the Old Madam says.”

Shen Old Madam smiled and patted the back of Shen Weici’s hand.

Song Zhang seemed equally out of place in the noisy gathering. He stared out at the lake through the pavilion windows. Even when Shen Siwen and Shen Yanli came to make conversation, he barely responded. The roasted meat the maidservants brought him sat untouched.

Only his gaze would drift, every now and then, from the window to Shen Weici — sitting at the Old Madam’s side with her eyes lowered and a smile at her lips.

Minhe, who stood at Song Zhang’s side, could not make sense of his general’s mind. At noon Song Zhang had come back to the estate saying he needed to change clothes before heading to the training grounds to drill and select men. Clearly that plan had been abandoned. But why was he sitting here of all places?

The roasted meat was gradually finished. Shen Weici had eaten only a piece or two.

It was the first time she had tried venison — it tasted good, though she was not used to it and found it somehow too gamey. Besides, only a small amount was roasted at once, and she always waited until everyone else had helped themselves first, so there was nothing left by the time it got to her.

The fruit wine, however, she found she liked well enough after a cup or two — the slight bitterness beneath the rich fragrance was somehow pleasing once you got used to it.

Whenever her cup was empty, a maidservant appeared to refill it. Without quite noticing, she had drunk three or four cups.

Outside, the rain grew heavier. It showed no sign of stopping.

The Old Madam had eventually grown tired, and was helped back to her rooms by an attendant matron.

Once the Old Madam was gone, those who remained felt free to talk as they pleased. After the roasted meat was finished, they started up a game of the Flying Flower Poetry Challenge, with ‘rain’ as the designated character. Anyone who could not produce a matching line would be penalized with wine.

The Flying Flower Challenge was not inherently difficult — one could cite lines from classical poets, or compose something on the spot.

But Shen Zhaozhao looked at Shen Weici and said they must compose something new on the spot; if you failed, the penalty was three cups.

She even looked pointedly at Shen Weici: “Third Younger Sister, you may not opt out.”

Shen Yanli saw this and said: “Third Younger Sister probably hasn’t had much formal schooling. Don’t make it hard for her — let’s keep the original rules.”

He turned to Shen Weici: “Third Younger Sister, don’t mind what Zhao-zhao says.”

Shen Weici sat beside the brazier. The warmth had brought a faint blush of pink to her fair cheeks, and her fingers, so cold earlier, had gradually thawed.

She heard Shen Yanli’s words and finally raised her eyes from their downward cast. She said lightly: “I will go along with whatever the elder and younger sisters decide. I only ask not to ruin everyone’s fun.”
