Matron Chang had also brought face powder, lip rouge, and blush — she set them on the table and smiled at Shen Weici: “The Second Lady says Third Young Miss has natural beauty. Even without making up your face you are lovely, but a little color would improve your complexion.”

Shen Weici put out a hand and stopped the matron’s fingers mid-reach toward her face: “Matron need not bother with that. Let us go now.”

Matron Chang’s hand froze in mid-air. She had not expected Shen Weici to stop her so directly.

She saw Shen Weici already standing and asking Yue Deng to fetch the cloak. She could only pick up the lip rouge: “At least let Third Young Miss put on this, then — it will give you more color.”

Shen Weici glanced at what Matron Chang was holding, and concealed the contempt that rose in her eyes. She said nothing more.

Matron Chang quickly applied the lip colour to Shen Weici’s lips. The previously bare, natural lips took on a deep crimson, and the already alluring face became suddenly more vivid.

Matron Chang stared for a moment. Truly a beauty to unsettle the heart.

Shen Weici did not speak more. She looked at Matron Chang and asked: “Are we leaving now?”

Matron Chang came to herself and went ahead to lead the way.

When they reached the front gate, Shen Rongsheng was unexpectedly waiting there.

Shen Weici went over to greet him with the same quiet obedience and asked: “Why is Father here at this hour?”

Shen Rongsheng looked at Shen Weici’s plainly dressed figure — though now there was no longer just that silver pin in her hair. A kingfisher-blue hairpin had replaced it, lending a touch of refinement.

He stood with his hands clasped behind him, the guilt in his heart spilling out of his eyes: “I came home from court early because I was uneasy. I wanted to see you.”

These words sounded as though they came from a caring and protective father.

Shen Weici’s eyes did not so much as flicker. She replied as she always did, gently and without any edge: “Daughter thanks Father for his concern.”

Shen Rongsheng sighed: “I know you are sensible. Having you go out to give this clarification is something we had no choice about. Do not blame your father.”

Shen Weici raised her face and shook her head: “Daughter understands Father also has his difficulties. She will not blame Father.”

Hearing Shen Weici’s words, the guilt inside Shen Rongsheng eased slightly. He called Shen Yanli over: “Accompany your Third Sister. Make sure she is looked after. No mistakes.”

Shen Yanli said: “Father, don’t worry. I go to that teahouse often. Nothing will go wrong.”

Only then did Shen Rongsheng nod with a small measure of relief.

chapters.title: He Came After All
chapters.content:
Standing at the front gate, Shen Rongsheng gave a few more instructions. Beside him, Lady Wen said: “The hour is about right, my lord. Let them go.”

Shen Zhaozhao, standing to one side, gave Shen Weici a cold look: “Remember clearly what you are supposed to say. If you say the wrong thing, do not expect me to let it pass when you return.”

Shen Rongsheng heard Shen Zhaozhao’s words and frowned, speaking low: “Zhaozhao, no more of that.”

Lady Wen caught the displeasure on Shen Rongsheng’s face and looked at Shen Weici: “All right, off you go.”

Shen Weici’s steps paused for a moment. Just before leaving, her previously downcast eyes lifted slightly toward her father: “Father — I am going.”

A strange sensation moved through Shen Rongsheng — as though calling up the memory of that old departure, when he had told that woman he would be back soon and she had sent him off with such gentle compliance, helping him dress and adjust his clothes.

Shen Rongsheng closed his eyes and sighed: “Go.”

Shen Weici lowered her eyes again and went toward the carriage.

Shen Zhaozhao watched Shen Weici’s figure disappear into the carriage curtain, and could not help whispering to her mother: “Can I go along and watch?”

Lady Wen patted Shen Zhaozhao’s hand: “That place is a mixed crowd of all kinds. What business does an unmarried girl have there? What if someone recognizes you?”

“Those people are not worthy of seeing you.”

Shen Zhaozhao nestled against her mother’s shoulder: “I just want to see how Shen Weici says it, in case she makes a mess of it.”

Lady Wen smiled: “Your elder brother is going along, and there are guards. She will not dare say the wrong thing.”

“And besides, Song Zhang’s men are not going — things might get unruly. If you were there and something happened to you, what then?”

Shen Rongsheng stood nearby, listening to the mother and daughter exchange these words. He watched the carriage gradually move away, and gave Lady Wen a cold, silent stare. He felt only a deepening revulsion for the woman beside him.

He told his attendant to prepare his own carriage, and made ready to go to the palace.

Lady Wen, struck by that look, stood watching his carriage recede down the alley without a word being spoken to her, and she felt, clearly, that Shen Rongsheng had grown colder and more distant these past days — nothing like the devoted, accommodating man who had always deferred to her in everything.

The handkerchief in her fingers was twisted tighter and tighter. All of this had changed the moment Shen Weici arrived.

Her eyes gradually went cold. Only when Shen Zhaozhao came to her side did she warm her expression again, and she took Shen Zhaozhao with her back inside.

Over at the teahouse, Shen Weici’s carriage drew up in front. Shen Yanli came down from the carriage behind and walked to Shen Weici’s curtain: “Third Sister, wait a moment. I will go up first and speak with the proprietor, and then speak with the storytellers.”

There was only a quiet “mm” from within before he took a few guards inside.

The moment he entered, he found the teahouse — usually bustling and noisy — completely silent. Every patron sat properly at their table, heads bowed over their tea, not daring to breathe too loudly.

He looked around. The entire three floors of the teahouse were lined with guards, whose sheer presence had silenced the room.

Looking toward the storytelling platform on the second floor, a dozen or so storytellers stood to one side, as though waiting for something.

Shen Yanli was delighted. He thought: Song Zhang must certainly be here. He went upstairs quickly, grabbed a tea server and asked: “Where is General Song?”

The server pointed in a direction. Shen Yanli looked — and there in a private booth across the floor, Song Zhang was seated in his usual grand and languid sprawl, with the teahouse proprietor attending nervously at his side.

Those indifferent eyes turned at that moment and landed on Shen Yanli.

Shen Yanli blinked, then went over quickly, and called a servant down to go and fetch Shen Weici.

Truly, getting Song Zhang to handle something was something else. Everything had been arranged perfectly.

The servant rushed down and delivered the message at the carriage curtain. Shen Weici heard and asked Matron Chang, in a mild tone: “Is there a gauze hat with a veil?”

Matron Chang was startled and replied before thinking: “Third Young Miss is meant to be seen by the people in the teahouse. If your face is covered, how can they believe you?”

Yue Deng could hold back no longer and stepped forward: “My young mistress has not yet married. If all those people in the teahouse see her face, what family of good standing would accept her afterward? This is a mixed crowd with all manner of people.”

“She is not refusing to go and clarify the matter. She can simply unveil at the end when she speaks. What is the harm in that?”

Matron Chang heard these words and could find no rebuttal. Every word was reasonable, and she had simply not thought of it when setting out.

She did not particularly care whether Shen Weici’s reputation was preserved — only that she achieve what her mistress needed. But now that the point had been raised, she could hardly tell her to just endure having everyone stare.

And yet — where was she to find a gauze veil hat right now?

She looked at Shen Weici with a manufactured expression of difficulty: “Third Young Miss’s concern is reasonable, but there is no veil hat now. Third Young Miss will simply have to bear with it.”

This was something that could be borne. Yue Deng was nearly boiling with anger, but Shen Weici’s soft fingers gripped hers.

She saw Shen Weici’s lovely eyes turn and fall on Matron Chang with a quiet, composed gaze. Her voice carried a trace of grievance: “Matron need not put herself to trouble. If the Manor’s face is more important than my own — then let it be more important. I will simply endure.”

And she lifted the carriage curtain and stepped out first.

Matron Chang watched Shen Weici’s retreating figure and felt a small jolt of wrongness. That tone had sounded quite genuinely aggrieved. She felt something was off and hurried to follow.

She went forward and asked: “Third Young Miss, what is the matter?”

Shen Weici looked up at her, pale: “Only that I have never been looked at by this many people.”

The fear in her looked unfeigned. Matron Chang was beginning to offer some comforting words when she realized Shen Weici had already bowed her head and was walking into the teahouse, and quickly hurried to stay close behind.

The moment they went in, they felt something was wrong. Why was it so quiet? Every patron sat with bowed head, as though afraid to look at the people coming in.

Shen Yanli was waiting by the door at this point. He saw Shen Weici enter and smiled: “Do not be afraid. Second Brother is here, and he has arranged everything well.”

Hearing that Song Zhang was also inside, Shen Weici gave a faint start, then lowered her brow and bit her lip, and nodded, following Shen Yanli toward the second-floor storytelling area.

chapters.title: Carried Away by Song Zhang
chapters.content:
The second floor was packed — yet every person there sat with their head down, silent as stone. Not even a breath was audible, for when that dark mass of Feathered Guard soldiers had entered earlier, they had said: listen only — do not look at the person. With the fearsome Cold Judge of the Feathered Guard seated above and watching, no one dared make a noise.

Shen Yanli felt an inexplicable gratification, though he puzzled at why no one was lifting their head. But he had no time to worry about it.

He walked beside Shen Weici as he guided her upstairs, bending toward her and saying: “Say what you need to say the same way Mother taught you this morning. Try to make it sound heartfelt, so people believe you. Once you have said it, I will take you home.”

He seemed to notice that Shen Weici’s color was poor — a faint dampness on her forehead as though she had broken into a light sweat. He bent to look at her more carefully: “Third Sister, are you all right?”

Yue Deng stepped forward and said quietly: “My young mistress is frightened. And this teahouse is full of men. Miss has not yet married — having this many people see her face is not right, and goes against propriety.”

“Just now I asked Matron Chang to find a veil hat for Miss, but she said there wasn’t one. So Miss had no choice but to come with her face uncovered. She must have been frightened by it.”

Shen Yanli heard this and saw the sense in it immediately. He had not considered Shen Weici’s reputation at all, only thought to have her come and clear the matter up.

But it was too late now to find a veil hat. He quickly reassured her: “It is all right. Say your piece and I will step in front of you when you are done, so as few people as possible see your face.”

Shen Weici then gave a pale nod.

Up in his booth, Song Zhang watched Shen Weici come upstairs. Shen Yanli bent close beside her, his tall frame almost entirely blocking her small figure from view — only the occasional glimpse of a pink skirt hem visible. Even that was enough to make his gaze linger.

His expression was cold, his sharp eyes never leaving Shen Weici for a moment. He seemed to be searching her quiet, fragile face for some trace of regret.

Regret for not having asked him for help.

But Song Zhang saw nothing. That gentle face was always composed.

Only when he was cruel to her did vulnerability show on it, and tears would tremble on the brink. Only then would she fix him with those indignant eyes.

And in front of Zhang Yuanheng she would wear a faintly shy smile, a becoming charm warming her cheeks.

The cup in his hand was gripped tighter and tighter. The darkness in his expression deepened, frightening the proprietor hovering nearby, who could not imagine what he himself had done wrong.

Until Shen Weici stood before the storyteller’s table — and the grip finally broke. Shards of porcelain fell one by one to the floor.

Shen Weici stood at the table with her head down, looking at the teacup Yue Deng placed before her. She raised it with delicate fingers and drank a light sip.

Shen Yanli smiled beside her: “Third Sister should wet her throat first.”

Shen Weici’s eyes moved, glancing at Shen Yanli, then back. She coughed twice.

Not loud, not soft — but in the hush of the teahouse the sound carried clearly.

Then Shen Weici began to speak. She said everything Lady Wen had instructed her to say that morning.

Her voice was pleasant — soft and clear, tinged with a faint coolness, her tone as gentle as river water, flowing steadily.

The listeners found themselves imagining, at the sound of that voice, a woman who must be cultured and gracious, good-tempered and beautiful — a proper lady of breeding.

But curious as they were, not one dared look up. They whispered furtively among themselves, feeling something suspicious about this whole arrangement.

What family would send their unmarried daughter out to show herself in a public place like this? From this one fact alone, the story of the Jian’an Marquis Manor mistreating its concubine-born daughter was probably not far from the truth. They had almost certainly forced the girl here.

Shen Yanli watched the reactions of those below with a vague satisfaction, thinking they would hold their tongues from now on.

He was thinking this when Yue Deng let out a piercing cry: “Miss — you are coughing blood again!”

The sound of it made Shen Yanli’s heart seize. He spun to look — and saw Shen Weici with one hand pressed on the table, the other gripping a handkerchief tightly to her mouth. The handkerchief was soaked red, and two drops of blood dripped from it — a sight to stop the heart.

Hearing Yue Deng’s shout, several people in the audience instinctively raised their heads. They did not see the face clearly, but they saw two hands stained with blood clutching a handkerchief to the lips, the cloth drenched red, bloodstains along the cuff of her sleeve.

What the audience saw was enough to make them reel. Someone cried out: “For the Jian’an Marquis Manor to treat an uncherished daughter like this — have they no conscience?!”

“They forced her here to make a public statement, and now she is coughing blood again — they are not human beings!”

“The Jian’an Marquis Manor is going to have a death on their hands! They are going to drive someone to her grave!”

Uproar broke out.

The Feathered Guard soldiers started forward to intervene — but Minhe waved them off. They halted at once and let the scene unfold.

And Song Zhang was no longer in his seat. He was already crossing the room toward Shen Weici — and seeing her fingers clenching into the edge of the table, the bloodstains at her fingers and collar, pain closed around his heart as though he could not breathe.

That copper-salt smell spreading outward — it made Song Zhang’s eyes go red.

He swept her up into his arms, kicked aside Shen Yanli who had gotten in the way, and with her held sideways against his chest he went striding rapidly down the stairs.

Yue Deng stood frozen for a moment, then came to her senses — Song Zhang was already downstairs with her young mistress.

Heart jumping, she rushed down the stairs after them.

Shen Yanli had never imagined things would turn out this way. He wanted to shout an explanation, but the people around him were already pressing toward him, furious, rolling up their sleeves.

Shen Yanli covered his head and ran — seeing the Feathered Guard also leaving with Song Zhang, he bellowed for his guards to form a line, then bolted through the back door in a panic.

Matron Chang was also caught in the surge and could not escape. She was seized by the agitated crowd and slapped twice before finally squeezing out — looking more or less like a battered pig’s head.

Yue Deng rushed out to find no trace of Song Zhang or her young mistress. She spotted Minhe coming out behind her and went straight to him: “Where is my mistress?”

Minhe looked at Yue Deng: “Your mistress coughed up that much blood — the General brought her away for her own good. Stop asking so many questions. Go home and wait for the General to send your mistress back.”

Yue Deng’s heart gave several rapid thumps. Her young mistress had only pretended to cough blood — if Song Zhang found out, it would be over.

She grabbed Minhe’s robe in desperate urgency: “I cannot manage without my young mistress. Could you take me to her?”

Minhe thought: I certainly cannot make that decision, and besides, a small maid like her could not hold him. He shook his sleeve free.

Mounted on his horse, he looked down at Yue Deng, on the verge of tears: “Do not be afraid. My General will not harm your young mistress.”

“In fact, by now the General has probably already called for a physician to see her.”

He rode off, leaving Yue Deng standing there even more terrified. She could only pray that Song Zhang would not figure it out.

She dared not even think what would happen if he did — her lord and his wife would know then that the previous time had also been a pretense, and the consequences would be beyond anything she could imagine.

chapters.title: I Will Not Let Anything Happen to You
chapters.content:
The carriage wheels outside turned at a rapid, urgent pace. Shen Weici, held tight in Song Zhang’s arms, came back to herself — and could barely catch her breath.

In her heart she had simply never expected Song Zhang to throw caution to the wind and carry her away. The situation now was more complicated than she had imagined.

She had the sense that Song Zhang was not easily fooled.

She had bitten through her tongue — there was real blood mixed in — but if the blood were examined closely, the color would not be quite deep enough. Without thinking, she tucked the handkerchief soaked with vermillion paint into her sleeve.

The light inside the carriage was dim. Song Zhang held Shen Weici pressed against his chest with his palm, and used his fingers to touch near her eyes.

Feeling the faint trembling of those lashes, Song Zhang’s grip tightened slightly. He said in a low voice: “Do not be afraid. I will have a physician come.”

“Nothing will happen to you.”

His words had barely fallen when he felt a soft hand catch his fingers. Then a quiet, slightly hoarse voice came: “Young Lord Song, taking me away like this — the Manor will be in an uproar…”

That voice was faint and thin — like a feather brushing across the heart. She always spoke in this careful, measured way, so pleasant to the ear.

And still worrying about whether the Manor was in an uproar.

Song Zhang took her hand in return. It was so small that he could close his entirely around it. He looked down at her face, half-lit and half-shadowed in the dim space of the carriage — at the faint trace of blood at the corner of her lip — and his voice, without his noticing, carried a certain gentleness: “Let it be in an uproar. I was the one who brought you away. Do you think such a small thing is beyond me to sort out?”

Shen Weici was startled. Her hand was held in Song Zhang’s and she could not pull free with force. She performed weakness: “I know Young Lord Song means well, but I cannot stay away — Father and Stepmother will worry.”

Song Zhang heard Shen Weici mention those cold-hearted parents and frowned, looking down at her: “Do you truly think they will worry? If they truly worried, let them worry. I will send you home when you are better, and no one will dare say a word.”

His fingertip brushed the corner of her lips, wiping away the trace of blood there, then cupped her lips with his palm. He said with some irritation: “You coughed up so much blood and you still have so much to say. Do you have any regard for your own health at all?”

A man’s large hand — broad and burning — its scorching warmth sent a flutter through Shen Weici’s heart.

She could not speak. Song Zhang’s other arm held tight around her shoulder. Her cheek was pressed against his chest, and the strong, steady heartbeat entered her ear one beat at a time — matching the unease she felt now.

This level of closeness should never have existed between them. But Song Zhang had done it to save her, and Shen Weici could not say anything against it. She only feared that so many people had seen — that it might give rise to gossip, and make finding a marriage even harder.

At this moment Song Zhang’s mind could only be described as wholly distracted. He knew well that Shen Weici had been ill and was not well, and yet he could not stop himself from thinking about how soft this body was, and even wanting to press it further.

Song Zhang was reckless by nature — he acted on his wishes. Only with Shen Weici did he feel himself constrained.

He thought her too tender and gentle — he was actually afraid of startling her.

He breathed in the faint blood-scent mixed with warmth that clung to her, and his heart quickened. Almost against his will, he bent just slightly, and held Shen Weici closer against him.

The carriage soon arrived at his private residence. Song Zhang carried her inside and went straight to his usual quarters. Minhe walked at his side and murmured: “Someone has been sent to the palace to fetch Imperial Physician Lin. He should arrive very soon.”

Song Zhang did not reply. His broad back blocked Minhe’s view as he carried Shen Weici inside.

Shen Weici did not know where Song Zhang had carried her to. Her mouth was full of blood — just now when Song Zhang had covered her lips she had been forced to swallow a mouthful of it, and her tongue ached terribly. She tugged at Song Zhang’s sleeve: “Let me go back to the Marquis Manor first.”

Song Zhang was not going to listen to a word of that. He carried her to the bed and set her down, drew the covers up around her, then sat at the bedside and looked at her pale face, at the blood-spatter on the pink collar of her robe, at those fine white fingers stained almost completely red.

The sight of it shook him every time.

He called for the maids to quickly bring warm water, and looked at the fingers still gripping tight to his sleeve, unable to understand why Shen Weici was so insistent on returning.

Her father and stepmother did not treat her very well.

His face was dark but his hands were gentle. He tucked aside the strands of hair that had fallen across her face, leaving that small, pale face completely unobstructed.

She was barely of age — and yet she carried at times a stillness that seemed beyond her years.

Song Zhang looked down and said, threatening her: “If you say the words ‘Marquis Manor’ one more time, I will throw you out into the street to fend for yourself.”

“Do not blame me then for having no pity.”

Shen Weici froze. She truly could not fathom Song Zhang’s intentions.

She knew that speaking further would only expose more. Her tongue was numb with pain, and without anything pressed against the wound, the blood kept coming. She glanced at Song Zhang, and thought: letting Song Zhang see more blood might make the pretense more convincing.

The blood in her mouth could not be held anymore. Shen Weici let herself pretend to bring up another small amount, tilted her head, and braced a hand on the edge of the bed, letting a small mouthful fall to the floor.

Her fingers trembled slightly as they pressed on the bed. Song Zhang’s eyes went red seeing it. He swept forward and pulled Shen Weici tight against him, then called toward the outside in a low, furious voice: “Get Imperial Physician Lin here now. Fast horses.”

Minhe, not knowing what had just happened inside, heard this and immediately went.

Song Zhang held Shen Weici in his arms, took the warm cloth a maid held out and used it to wipe the blood from the corner of her mouth. His large hand moved gently up and down her back: “I will make sure nothing happens to you.”

Shen Weici tried to push Song Zhang away, knowing she should not be capable of that kind of strength. She rested her cheek against his shoulder and said in a weak voice: “Young Lord Song, please let go of me first. This is not proper.”

Song Zhang was so frustrated he nearly felt his own blood rising — he said through clenched teeth: “You are in this state, and you are still talking about what is proper? I am, by blood relations, close enough to count as your cousin. A man cannot hold a little sister?”

“If anyone in this room dares say a word about it, I will cut out their tongue and gouge out their eyes.”

At these words, the maids standing in attendance dared not so much as glance sideways, and hurriedly lowered their eyes in unison.

The warm fragrance he had been dreaming of was right beside him now, soft breathing falling at his neck. Song Zhang felt a sweet, languid ache in his heart — and then he looked down and saw the blood Shen Weici had coughed up, and the tenderness wrung at him just as sharply.

He held her greedily, his fingers resting on her slender waist, holding her close and protected.

Whether it was private longing or that thread of genuine tenderness, Song Zhang would not release her — not a single fingertip.

Imperial Physician Lin arrived to find Song Zhang holding Shen Weici tightly in his arms. He immediately lowered his eyes and did not dare look further, bowing respectfully toward Song Zhang: “General Song.”

Song Zhang’s expression went cold the moment he saw Imperial Physician Lin. He had been the one who came last time as well, and the prescription he wrote had been completely useless — the girl had coughed blood again.

If it were not for the immediate need to save someone, Song Zhang could have kicked Imperial Physician Lin half to death on the spot.

chapters.title: Second Cousin, I Don’t Want to Die
chapters.content:
Even the slightest hardening of Song Zhang’s gaze was enough to carry a breath of murderous intent. He had killed men on the frontier before he was ten years old, and the killing aura that had settled in him over the years was enough to drench Senior Imperial Physician Lin in cold sweat, buckle his knees, and very nearly bring him to the floor.

Song Zhang set Shen Weici down on the couch, stood, and told a maidservant to lower the curtain. Then he gripped Shen Weici’s hand and fixed Imperial Physician Lin with a frigid stare. “Take a proper look this time. Why has she coughed up blood again?”

His voice dropped colder still. “If you can’t get her well again, don’t bother going back to the Imperial Medical Office. I’ll have you sent straight to the canal troops as a footstool.”

Everyone knew the canal labor corps was the most punishing and exhausting posting in the empire. A man of his constitution would not last a month.

Imperial Physician Lin was so frightened by Song Zhang’s words that he quickly said, “General Song, rest assured — this official will examine the patient with all care and diligence.”

Only then did he dare step forward and stoop to take Shen Weici’s pulse.

Song Zhang remained standing at his side the whole time, that wordless pressure of his bearing making Imperial Physician Lin’s heart pound with terror. He was half-convinced that if this lord of death took one wrong mood, the sword would be out.

But the pulse beneath his fingers did not register any violent agitation — quite the contrary, it was even and unhurried, somewhat steadier than the last time he had examined her.

He could not fathom why she had coughed blood again, and unease stirred in his chest.

He released her wrist and chose his words carefully. “Third Miss Shen’s pulse is still indicating suppressed stagnation. The liver qi is slightly dominant, affecting the heart and spleen — it should respond to treatment.”

Song Zhang heard this and let out a cold laugh. He reached to the side of his waist and drew his sword in one clean motion. The flash of cold steel was enough to send Imperial Physician Lin shaking to his knees, screaming for mercy.

Song Zhang leveled the long blade against Lin’s throat. The sword had been dipped in countless men’s blood, and its killing aura was such that simply bringing it near skin was enough to leave a faint red line from the edge alone.

Song Zhang’s voice came out like ice. “You said exactly this to me last time. The pills you prescribed were useless, and here she is coughing blood again this soon. Were you going to try feeding me that same answer twice?”

Imperial Physician Lin had no defense to offer and nothing else he could truthfully say. He remained on his knees, begging for his life.

Just when he had convinced himself he was about to die here, a soft, slightly husky voice sounded from within: “Young Master Song — it is not his fault.”

Imperial Physician Lin could not help but look up. A slender hand lifted the curtain, then a sleeve of smoky pink emerged, and then a face — gentle and lovely, yet with a complexion somewhat drained of color, the lips startlingly red against the pallor, their corners still touched with a haze of blood. The contrast of fragility and strange vividness made him stare for a moment in spite of himself.

So this was the Third Miss Shen the rumors spoke of — the one the Jian’an Marquis household had seen fit to marry off to Zhang Tingyi, never treating her as one of their own. And yet she was stunning. The Marquis household was truly capable of wasting this.

Though this constitution of hers — coughing blood at the slightest provocation — was ultimately a liability. No great family would want to take in a wife like this.

Song Zhang stopped short. He turned his head and saw that Shen Weici had lifted the curtain. Her trembling eyes were calm as still water. Then he heard her say: “The medicine Young Master Song gave me — I never took it.”

Song Zhang’s expression darkened at once, and he narrowed his eyes at her with displeasure. “You refused to take what I gave you?”

Shen Weici could barely withstand the chill in Song Zhang’s gaze. She lowered her eyes gently and spoke in a measured voice. “It was not that I refused. When my maidservant was giving it to me, she accidentally dropped it into the water, and it could not be taken.”

Her voice was thick and indistinct — every word she spoke sent a piercing ache through her.

Song Zhang bit down, his hands trembling with suppressed anger. His fingers twitched. He looked at Shen Weici in this state and held himself back from any further roughness toward her. He bent at the waist, bringing his face close to hers, and asked through clenched teeth: “Shen Weici, do you take me for a fool?”

Shen Weici met Song Zhang’s phoenix eyes at close range. Those eyes — perhaps because they had seen too many deaths — always carried a trace of careless indifference to life and limb. When they narrowed, they became rather frightening, as though he might snap her neck in the next moment.

She was, if she were honest, somewhat unnerved by Song Zhang’s gaze. It was sharp and utterly composed, the kind of look that would not yield to anyone — no one who met it head-on could hold their ground.

She blinked softly, pressed her sleeve over her lips, coughed up another thread of blood, and drew a quiet breath. Her eyes met his. “Young Master Song — I don’t want to die.”

“I have no reason not to take it.”

Shen Weici’s words — I don’t want to die — combined with the blood she coughed into her sleeve and the weakness of her voice, struck every taut nerve in Song Zhang’s body.

There had never been a moment in his life when he had felt so completely at a loss for what to do.

He took the handkerchief from a maidservant nearby and, with some irritation and considerable gracelessness, dabbed at the corner of Shen Weici’s mouth. The irritation in his voice sounded more like anger directed at himself. He gripped her shoulders tightly and looked at the blood spreading across her lips: “Fine. I believe you — is that what you want?”

Shen Weici heard the vexation in Song Zhang’s voice and looked at his grim expression, then lowered her eyes and said nothing more.

Song Zhang sheathed his sword, then delivered a kick to Imperial Physician Lin’s ribs where the man was still kneeling on the floor. “Are you going to write the prescription and have the medicine decocted, or not? If she isn’t well again after this, don’t bother going back to the Imperial Medical Office.”

Imperial Physician Lin did not want to remain there a single moment longer. He scrambled to his feet and bolted.

He had given everyone quite a fright.

Song Zhang sat down at the edge of the bed and, having no real notion of how to care for someone, moved with what he thought was gentleness — though the touch that landed on Shen Weici’s face was anything but tender.

His wiping left a red mark across that porcelain skin, and he muttered a complaint: “What sort of skin is this? One light pass and it goes red.”

He fixed her with a cold, sardonic look. “I wouldn’t have pegged you for a girl from the countryside. You seem more like something that fell from heaven.”

“It must be quite beneath you to be a concubine-born daughter of a Marquis household.”

Shen Weici heard the mockery in Song Zhang’s words, said nothing, and did not argue. She only reached out with one finger toward the handkerchief in his hand. Through the pain she said: “I can do it myself.”

Her light, soft fingers covered his. Only then did he truly understand what was meant by the phrase ‘fingers like soft silk.’

His heart began to pound, and even the cold line of his lips and the set of his brows softened just a little.

Yet his expression remained arrogant. He held the handkerchief stubbornly and gave a cold sniff. “I don’t make a habit of waiting on women. Don’t be ungrateful.”

Shen Weici was briefly taken aback. She genuinely could not follow the logic of Song Zhang’s moods.

But she had no wish to say more right now. The wound on her tongue was torturing her with every syllable, and since Song Zhang showed no sign of leaving, she could not hold the cloth in her mouth to stanch it — she had to simply endure the blood filling her mouth.

Song Zhang watched Shen Weici’s fingers withdraw. The warmth against his hand disappeared, and with it the faint scent she carried — even with the undercurrent of blood. Only she remained: her eyes closed, her fingers lying limp on the brocade quilt with no more life in them than a wilted flower.

He looked at her face with a slight, helpless stupor. He watched her close her eyes, and thought how striking that beauty mark above her lid looked in this moment.

Those lips so red, that face so coolly composed, those perfumed fingers — every one of these things plucked at his nerves.

The corner of her mouth had been rubbed red by his wiping — the color there now looked strangely intimate, as though someone had just been rough with her.

He reached out, and his thumb moved of its own accord to rest against Shen Weici’s lips. His throat worked. His mind went blank. Every last shred of pride and dignity fled to the back of his mind.

chapters.title: Wanting to Kiss Her
chapters.content:
The light outside came in through the window paper and fell onto Shen Weici’s closed eyes, giving that fringe of long lashes another layer of luminous color.

Song Zhang watched her with an aching sort of focus, his thumb sliding of its own accord to rest against Shen Weici’s full lips, his body bending closer to her.

Shen Weici had assumed Song Zhang was simply wiping the last of the blood from the corner of her mouth. It was only when his breath fell over her in a wave of heat that she was mildly startled and opened her eyes.

Their gazes met. Song Zhang paused — and only then registered what he had been about to do. He had been about to kiss her.

The involuntary impulse infuriated him, and Shen Weici’s expression in that moment only made the sense of rebuke worse.

He shot to his feet and looked down at her with cold detachment. “Don’t read anything into that. You happen to have a very small mole just below your lip. I was curious and looked close.”

Shen Weici had not actually thought anything of it. She did have a small mole below her lip — very faint, so slight that most people would never notice.

She blinked. “I didn’t think anything.”

But those words, given so readily and without any resistance, sat wrong with Song Zhang in a way he could not account for. He did not know where this new irritation came from.

Every time he saw Shen Weici, he felt a formless anger flare up — and yet he kept wanting to come closer.

Song Zhang said nothing more. He kept his face stormy and stopped looking at Shen Weici, then turned and walked out with long strides.

Shen Weici breathed a quiet sigh of relief to see the last of Song Zhang’s back. Out of the corner of her eye she noticed several maidservants still standing in the room, and she asked in a low voice whether any of them had a clean, unused handkerchief.

She had asked without much hope — this was Song Zhang’s residence by the look of it, and there would almost certainly be no woman’s kerchief here. As for the maidservants having an unused one of their own — that also seemed unlikely.

But when the words were out, one of the girls said she did — and promptly left to fetch it.

Physically, Shen Weici felt nothing especially wrong. Only her tongue ached unbearably, sending cold sweat pricking to the surface with every throb of pain. She remembered that last time it had taken three days before it improved, and this time would probably be about the same.

She buried herself in the quilt. She could not go anywhere right now, so she might as well sleep. Whatever commotion was happening outside at this moment had very little to do with her.

Even Song Zhang appeared to have believed her. There was probably no one who suspected the truth.

She had already told Yue Deng what to say. There was nothing in their account that could be picked apart.

Before long the maidservant returned with a fresh handkerchief. She found Shen Weici had lain down and bent over her. “Miss?”

Shen Weici had not fully fallen asleep. She heard the voice and accepted the handkerchief. She had been about to ask where Song Zhang had gone and whether he was coming back, then thought better of it — these few maidservants would probably have no idea.

She pulled the quilt over her head, pressed the handkerchief against the wound in her mouth, and told herself if she held steady pressure long enough, the bleeding would stop.

When Song Zhang came back in, he found Shen Weici with her head completely buried under the quilt, as though she were asleep.

He had never seen anyone sleep like this. Frowning, he reached out and yanked the quilt back, uncovering the face she had muffled inside.

Her small face had been so thoroughly smothered that it had turned pink. Her already charming features had a blurred, spring-water softness to them now, the flush at the outer corners of her eyes suffused with a warm ambiguity. Song Zhang stared.

He leaned down and reached to feel Shen Weici’s forehead — not hot, only slightly damp, as though she had been too warm under the covers.

He looked at the medicine a maidservant had brought and, seeing Shen Weici apparently deep in sleep, wondered whether or not to wake her.

Shen Weici was in fact fully awake. She simply had not expected Song Zhang to come back in and pull the quilt off her immediately. She had not had time to take the cloth from her mouth, and explaining it would be awkward — so she pretended to sleep.

Song Zhang stood at the bedside for a moment and decided: she was in no condition to skip medicine. He sat down at the head of the bed.

Shen Weici felt a shadow fall over her, and then a large hand slid beneath her. Before she could quite register what was happening, Song Zhang had gathered her up into his arms.

His arm circled her from the side, her back pressed against his chest. A spoonful of medicine was brought to her lips — he was evidently intending to feed it to her.

She had no choice but to open her eyes. The first thing she saw, upon doing so, was Song Zhang holding the medicine bowl in one hand and a spoon in the other, about to feed her.

Her mind went blank for an instant. She could not fathom why Song Zhang was attending to her like this today.

He certainly did not look like someone who knew how to look after people.

She still had something in her mouth and could not drink just yet. She turned her face slightly to the side, deflecting the spoonful of medicine Song Zhang was offering.

Song Zhang’s impatient voice came from above her head. “Don’t be ungrateful. I don’t have a great deal of patience for spoon-feeding people.”

Shen Weici stiffened, and had no choice but to take the cloth from her mouth.

It was soaked through with blood. Before Song Zhang could ask, she had her answer ready: “There was too much blood in my mouth.”

Song Zhang had a maidservant remove the bloodied handkerchief, then frowned and looked at the corner of Shen Weici’s mouth. “Did it not occur to you to ask someone to bring you tea to rinse with?”

Speaking again had drawn a fresh trickle from the wound on her tongue. She lowered her eyes and said hoarsely: “I forgot.”

Song Zhang let out a cold laugh. “You’re sharp enough most of the time — you play the dice-board game with your own ingenuity, you knew to play dumb at the flying-flower poetry match with Shen Zhaozhao, and you had plenty of tricks for snaring Zhang Yuanheng. But rinsing your own mouth is something you forgot?”

“I’m no longer sure whether you’re cleverly pretending to be foolish, or just actually foolish.”

Shen Weici heard Song Zhang bring up luring Zhang Yuanheng again and felt no inclination whatsoever to defend herself.

Besides, any future with Zhang Yuanheng was no longer possible.

Song Zhang watched Shen Weici sit in silence, her soft body still leaning against him — apparently quite content to do as she was told — and yet he was furious with her for the shy, tender way she had looked at Zhang Yuanheng. Every line she had written urging Zhang Yuanheng to come and propose had rankled him.

He set the medicine bowl into a maidservant’s hands and reached for the teacup instead, holding it to Shen Weici’s lips without any particular warmth. “Rinse.”

Shen Weici reached out with both hands to take the cup from him, but he would not release it. She had to open her mouth and take in a sip, then turn her head slightly to spit it into the small vessel a maidservant held nearby.

What came out was tinged pink. Song Zhang watched, his lips pressing into a tight line.

He fed her the medicine next. Shen Weici could not refuse it, and she drank it down obediently, without protest.

The warm liquid rolling over the wound burned in a way that only she would know. She endured it in silence, telling herself she would talk about going home that afternoon.

Song Zhang was nominally her cousin, so it was not entirely improper for her to be here. But she was worried about Yue Deng managing alone.

Song Zhang had no real method when it came to feeding someone. He sent each spoonful straight in — far too large — and Shen Weici frequently could not swallow fast enough, and medicine ran from the corner of her mouth down her jaw into the collar of her robe.

Song Zhang actually complained that Shen Weici’s mouth was too small, and the maidservants watching nearby were quietly frantic — there would be spills even with a perfectly proportioned spoon fed at this pace. It was truly a credit to Third Miss Shen’s composure that she endured it without a word of protest.

One of the maidservants tried to step in and help, only to have Song Zhang’s cold gaze pin her hand in midair. She withdrew it, frightened, and would not try again — though she shot Shen Weici a quietly sympathetic look.

Song Zhang himself, however, felt perfectly satisfied. Attending to her like this ought to feel like a privilege to her. He was doing something he had never done for anyone in twenty-two years of life.

chapters.title: I’ve Never Seen Anyone More Delicate Than You
chapters.content:
The collar of Shen Weici’s robe was faintly damp where medicine had trickled from the corner of her lips. When she had finally finished the whole bowl, she noticed that Song Zhang still held her with no sign of releasing her, and after a moment she asked: “Won’t Young Master Song be going to the Palace today?”

Song Zhang oversaw the Forbidden Guard, but this did not require him to appear at the Palace every single day. His subordinates handled the daily arrangements for all watch rotations, and he himself would stop by the Vice-Commander’s Residence, or go to the training ground to drill his troops, or attend whenever the Emperor summoned him or needed an escort. He had, at his leisure, no very pressing schedule.

Shen Weici’s voice was faint, as though she had something in her mouth, blurring the words a little — but to Song Zhang’s ears it carried an unmistakable note of impatience. She sounded as if she found his presence an overstay.

He dismissed all the maidservants from the room, then finally looked down at Shen Weici’s face. He noticed, only now, the dampness along her jaw — and looking further, the wet stain on her collar.

He paused, looking at her still-downcast eyes. “Why didn’t you tell me to slow down?”

Shen Weici’s pale eyes did not so much as lift. Yet she answered him in her customary unhurried, courteous way. “Young Master Song rescued me. I ought to be grateful. How could I fault him for feeding me too quickly?”

Song Zhang stilled. He looked at the sharp, fine point of Shen Weici’s chin and those cherry-red lips, still glistening wet, her mole at the outer corner of her eye graceful and vivid.

He could not tell whether this was genuine gratitude or simply the polished pleasantries she always produced. Either way, something stirred in him — moved by her endurance of it, her quiet self-containment.

Song Zhang reached out and tilted Shen Weici’s chin up to make her look at him. The skin under his fingers was faintly damp. He looked into her eyes, searching for something beyond the surface — some other emotion — and found he could not read her at all.

His thumb moved against her smooth, soft skin. Song Zhang wanted to kiss her — wanted to see her expression if he did — wanted to know whether she would lean into him.

He leaned gradually closer. His eyes, though cold, had a heart beating fast behind them.

And yet just as his lips were about to brush against hers, Shen Weici coughed.

Her pale, smooth fingers came up to cover her mouth. Both slender brows pinched together, a faint damp sheen appearing at her temples. She coughed several times in a row, and looked genuinely wretched.

Song Zhang quickly raised his hand and began to pat Shen Weici’s back with gentle strokes. He frowned and said in a low, gruff voice: “How did you end up with a constitution this weak? What exactly were you living on in Yuyang?”

“I’ve never seen anyone more delicate than you.”

He caught himself halfway and looked at Shen Weici’s face. She had lowered her gaze again, still as ever, as though she had not heard a word he said. But that quiet discomfort at the corners of her eyes — her brows soft as misty rain — made his throat tighten, and the contemptuous words died on his tongue.

His fingers tightened against her slender waist. He did not want to let go, yet had no real justification for continuing to hold her. Looking at her damp collar, the faint sheen on her forehead, and the body that seemed to have no support of its own, he reasoned to himself that he felt sorry for her — that he was holding her because she was pitiable, and keeping her a little longer was simply a matter of comfort, because she had no one close at hand to attend to her.

Besides, they were nominally cousins — some distant degree of family. What was wrong with holding her? And there were no maidservants watching.

Even with all this reasoning in place, he could not stop himself from looking down at Shen Weici’s face — and when he failed to find the fearful, resistant expression he had half expected, he found the corners of his mouth turning upward before he could prevent it.

The smell of her was wonderful. If not for the necessity of keeping up appearances, Song Zhang would have buried his face in her neck and simply breathed her in.

Even with the trace of blood, she smelled wonderful.

He reached for her collar, and said with perfect composure: “Your collar is loose. I’ll straighten it — it must be uncomfortable pressed against you like that.”

Shen Weici had no idea what Song Zhang was trying to do. Her pallid face contracted, and she closed her hand around Song Zhang’s fingers where they had wandered to her collar. She looked up and said quietly: “Young Master Song, I’m rather tired.”

Shen Weici’s hand was small and soft. To Song Zhang it felt no more than a light scratch.

He raised an eyebrow at her. “If Third Miss Shen is tired, she need only sleep. Surely Third Miss Shen doesn’t sleep in her outer garments?”

“Since I am the one who brought Third Miss Shen here, it falls to me to attend to her.”

His long fingers had already undone one of the buttons at Shen Weici’s collar.

Shen Weici’s expression shifted. She gripped her collar with her fingers and looked at Song Zhang. “Please don’t trouble yourself. I’ll have a maidservant help me.”

Song Zhang had genuinely meant nothing by it — he simply did not want the damp collar pressing against her uncomfortably.

But the wariness in Shen Weici’s eyes brought him up short. He muttered under his breath about ingratitude, released her, laid her against the soft pillow, and went out with irritation clenched in his chest. He called two maidservants in to see to her.

Outside, Minhe came to Song Zhang’s side and lowered his voice. “Second Young Master Shen has come, General. He is asking urgently for Third Miss.”

Song Zhang looked at him and settled into the armchair in the outer room. “Did he come alone?”

Minhe nodded. “He says the Marquis household is in an uproar. The Old Madam has also sent word asking you to bring Third Miss back — she wishes to speak with Third Miss in person.”

Song Zhang’s expression darkened. He asked flatly: “Speak with her about what.”

Minhe thought for a moment. “I expect the General knows — it would be about what happened in the teahouse this morning.”

“The scene at the teahouse was witnessed by quite a few people, including several of the storytellers who perform there. I had a word with them, and by now the rumors about the Jian’an Marquis household are spreading faster than before.”

“People are saying the Marquis household first sold off a daughter for social advancement, and then forced the girl to make a public spectacle of herself in a teahouse to recant her words. That the Second Branch of the Jian’an Marquis household has rotten hearts and exhausted every wickedness, and would soon receive their due.”

Minhe looked at Song Zhang. “These rumors are going a little far. The Jian’an Marquis household’s reputation may well be ruined. Should I ask the storytellers to show some restraint and stop spreading things further?”

Song Zhang gave a cold laugh. “Let them keep going.”

Before the conversation was finished, a guard came in and reported, kneeling: “General, a messenger has come from the Palace asking you to attend immediately. His Majesty wishes to see you now.”

Song Zhang listened without visible reaction. He had already formed a rough guess about the nature of the summons. He rose from the chair, looked at Minhe: “Stay here and send Shen Yanli away.”

“And if anything happens to her, have word sent to me in the Palace. Don’t let her leave. Make sure the afternoon medicine is not forgotten.”

Minhe nodded quickly. “The General may go without worry.”

Song Zhang, satisfied that everything was arranged, swept his robe aside and strode out.

chapters.title: Called to Account
chapters.content:
Inside Jian’an Marquis Estate, Yue Deng was kneeling in the main hall of the Old Madam’s Cishou Hall. Above her sat Old Madam Shen, with the Second Madam and Second Master and Second Young Miss seated to either side. Behind her two formidable matrons loomed, close enough to make a cold sweat prick at her forehead.

There came a dull thud from above — a teacup set down hard against a table — and then Old Madam Shen’s voice, full of authority: “You will explain yourself properly. What happened today?”

“The Imperial Physician has been in and out, and she has been taking medicine all these days. How is it that she has coughed blood again?”

At this, Shen Zhaozhao could contain herself no longer. “Grandmother, does it not strike anyone as altogether too convenient that Shen Weici would cough blood at precisely the critical moment? The rumors outside are even worse than before because of it. I say she did it on purpose!”

Yue Deng, hearing Shen Zhaozhao’s accusation, immediately kowtowed through tears. “Old Madam, Second Master, Second Madam — in all honesty, my young miss would never dare do such a thing deliberately.”

“Last night, Madam Chang — Second Madam’s attendant — came to Linchun Courtyard and told my young miss to go to Second Young Master Song’s quarters and ask him to send someone. At that point my young miss had only just finished bathing, and her hair was not yet fully dry. Madam Chang was pressing her, and she was afraid of being late, so she endured and went.”

“It is the dead of winter, and bitterly cold. My young miss went outside with her hair still wet and walked through cold wind the whole way there. By the time she returned, her head was throbbing — she barely slept that night.”

“When she rose early the following morning to pay her respects to Second Madam, she came back looking wrong in the face. But my young miss endured it without a word, not wanting to cause any delays.”

“At the teahouse today, my young miss asked Madam Chang for a veil hat. The teahouse was full of people, and since my young miss is an unmarried young lady, being seen by so many people was not proper.”

“But Madam Chang said that people needed to see her, otherwise no one would believe it — and that the face of the Marquis household came first.”

“My young miss has always been thin-skinned. She heard those words and kept her silence. After entering the teahouse she was trembling from head to foot. Even Third Young Master noticed she was not right and told my young miss to hold on a little longer.”

Yue Deng’s voice broke into fresh sobs as she pressed her forehead to the floor once more, then looked up at Shen Rongsheng through her tears. “My young miss has suffered from a cold affliction since childhood, and she keeps everything inside. However wronged she may be, she will not say a word. She has not once cried out.”

“Since coming to the Marquis household, my young miss has reminded me over and over to keep the rules, to listen to the Old Madam and the Masters and Madams, and not to make trouble.”

“The Imperial Physician said last time that my young miss’s coughing of blood was a result of long-suppressed grief and depleted vital energy. This time, she bore it all — stood in front of all those people without flinching, delivered every single word Second Madam had instructed her to deliver, without missing one — and only at the very last moment, when she could no longer endure it, did the blood come up.”

“But the coughing of blood is not something my young miss can control. Third Young Master was beside her and saw it himself. It could not be faked.”

“My young miss was taken away by Second Young Master Song, and I did not expect that. I beg the Old Madam, Second Master, and Second Madam to consider clearly: my young miss is devoted to the Marquis household. Even though she was not willing to marry Master Zhang, she still, for the sake of the greater situation, returned the betrothal items sent by the Earldom household, and has been quietly waiting to be married off.”

When Yue Deng finished speaking, the great hall fell into complete silence. No one knew how to begin.

Yue Deng was a maidservant, and yet every word she had said was reasoned and orderly, logically sound. Listening to it, one could only feel she was in the right.

The coughing of blood was indeed beyond a person’s control, and besides, making an unmarried young lady stand in a teahouse full of all manner of strangers was something even an ordinary person might find difficult to bear.

Shen Zhaozhao’s expression curdled. Seeing that no one spoke, she stood directly from her seat, walked to stand beside Yue Deng, and pointed at her. “What a glib-tongued maidservant. But clever as you are, you just made a slip.”

Yue Deng was taken aback. “Every word I said is the truth, without fabrication.”

Shen Zhaozhao laughed coldly and stood before Yue Deng. “You just said that your young miss also didn’t want to marry Zhang Tingyi. Doesn’t that mean her whole show of compliance was entirely false?”

“Perhaps she hates the Marquis household, hates my father and mother — and so she arranged all of this in the teahouse on purpose, to set the people outside talking and condemning us.”

“Now that your young miss has gotten what she wanted, is she sitting at Second Elder Brother’s place right now watching the Marquis household make a spectacle of itself?”

Shen Zhaozhao’s argument made the expressions around the room, which had just begun to soften in Yue Deng’s favor, harden again. Every gaze swung back to Yue Deng.

Yue Deng’s face went white. She kowtowed through her choked voice. “Second Young Miss, why must you wrong my young miss this way?”

“When Second Master originally planned a match for my young miss with Master Zhang of the Yiyong Earldom, my young miss had already developed a mutual regard with Master Zhang and naturally did not wish to marry Master Zhang of the later proposal. On the day both the Earldom household and the Zhang household came to formally propose at the same time, my young miss, for the sake of the greater situation, asked the Earldom household to leave first.”

“If my young miss had truly been hoping to expose the Marquis household to mockery, she would not have sent the Earldom household away. Having both parties collide on the doorstep at the same time would have made a far greater spectacle, wouldn’t it?”

Before the last word was fully out of Yue Deng’s mouth, a matron’s hand caught her across the face. “How dare you, you insolent little slave — speaking to your betters that way!”

Yue Deng pressed her hand to her cheek, weeping with a grief that broke the heart, and looked toward Second Master Shen Rongsheng in desperate appeal. “Second Master — my young miss has had too hard a life. She came to the Marquis household and has been careful at every turn. She has never had any other intentions. I beg the Second Master to see clearly.”

Shen Rongsheng heard Yue Deng’s final words, and his expression paused.

He had never looked too closely into what kind of life Shen Weici had lived in Yuyang before coming here. She had mentioned it once, and the picture she painted had not been good.

Since coming to the Marquis household, she had been quiet and unobtrusive, never stirring up any trouble. Suddenly arranging her marriage to Zhang Tingyi had, in truth, been a wrong done to her by his own hand.

Zhang Yuanheng had been a proper match for her. If it had not been for his mother and Madam Wen privately contriving to marry Shen Weici to Zhang Tingyi, none of this mess would have come about.

When he traced it back, it all came down to Madam Wen — that woman was incapable of tolerating anyone who threatened her interest, and could not bear to see Shen Weici live even a tolerable life.

And then he thought of what the Emperor had said when he detained him at court this morning: “It is time to attend to private virtue.”

The words had put fear in him, a gnawing feeling that disaster was coming.

Now the rumors outside had grown beyond anyone’s ability to stop them. He feared that by tomorrow, the memorials impeaching him would be even more numerous. As for how to explain things to Zhang Yuanheng, he had not the faintest idea. He was utterly overwhelmed.

He had spent the whole journey home turning the Emperor’s words over in his mind. He had finally arrived at his conclusion: the Emperor had himself grown exasperated at the sight of him marrying a daughter off to an aging widower.

The great hall was silent except for the muffled sound of Yue Deng’s suppressed sobbing. Madam Wen glanced at Yue Deng, who would not stop wiping at her eyes, then looked at Shen Rongsheng. “I think Zhao-zhao’s argument has some merit.”

“How is it that Shen Weici was so obediently willing to marry Zhang Tingyi?”

Shen Rongsheng heard those words and felt the fuse that had been buried in him for a very long time finally ignite. He stood up and struck Madam Wen across the face. “You vicious woman! You know perfectly well Weici didn’t want to marry Zhang Tingyi.”

“Then why did you go behind my back to arrange this match?”

“Weici had barely arrived in this household before you were scheming against her. Now look what you’ve done to everything — are you satisfied?”

“The entire court is sending up memorials condemning me — saying I sold a daughter for favor, saying I drove my own flesh and blood to her grave, saying I married a heartless shrew who has turned the household into a battleground.”

“I’m about to lose the hat on my head, and you — you are satisfied?”

Madam Wen reeled backward from Shen Rongsheng’s blows, nearly collapsing onto the floor. She stared at the face of the man before her, which she had never once seen look like this in all their years of marriage — contorted with fury, screaming her faults at her in front of everyone, all for Shen Weici’s sake.

She raised a trembling finger at Shen Rongsheng. “I set out every consideration for you that day. I told you, if you weren’t afraid of offending Zhang Tingyi, refuse him outright. In the end it was you who agreed to the match. You agreed to marry Shen Weici to Zhang Tingyi.”

Shen Rongsheng heard Madam Wen dare to turn the blame on him, and his rage erupted. “You foolish woman! If you hadn’t taken Weici to the Zhang household to ingratiate yourself in the first place, would any of this have followed?!”

Madam Wen recoiled at Shen Rongsheng’s shout and immediately threw herself weeping toward Old Madam Shen. “Old Madam, please take a stand! My husband is laying all the blame on me, but this isn’t fair — it was never my idea, and I never insisted that Shen Weici marry Zhang Tingyi. How has everything become my fault alone?”

Old Madam Shen heard what Madam Wen was getting at. She knew. She had been the one who first proposed it. Properly speaking, it was not Madam Wen’s fault at all.

Her eyes turned sharp and fixed on Shen Rongsheng. “What is all this commotion for? The situation is what it is — the task now is to find a way to resolve it.”

“As long as Zhang Tingyi still intends to marry Shen Weici, this remains workable.”

“Noble Consort Zhang has enjoyed sole imperial favor for many years. As long as the Emperor does not censure us, what do a few memorials of impeachment amount to?”

“Once Shen Weici is married into the Zhang household, we and the Zhang family become relatives by marriage. If she produces an heir, the connection grows even closer. Would Noble Consort Zhang not look after you?”

“Those outside rumors amount to nothing. They won’t overturn heaven.”

Those words were the last remaining reassurance anyone had to offer — if Zhang Tingyi still intended the marriage, everything remained negotiable.

Shen Rongsheng gave a cold laugh. “Is the Emperor’s authority greater, or Zhang Tingyi’s? The Emperor himself has told me my private conduct is lacking. And now I’m supposed to go ahead and marry my daughter off to Zhang Tingyi?”

Old Madam Shen was startled by his words and was about to ask for more detail when Shen Yanli came rushing in. She quickly asked: “Is Weici at Song Zhang’s?”

Shen Yanli caught his breath, took a large gulp of tea that someone handed him, and then replied: “Third Younger Sister is at Second Elder Brother Song’s place. But he won’t release her. He says Third Younger Sister is gravely ill, and if she comes back she’ll only be driven to her death — she’s better off recovering at his place.”

Old Madam Shen heard this and nearly choked with fury. “What does Song Zhang mean by this? What does he mean, driven to her death?”

Shen Yanli hunched his shoulders and looked at the Old Madam. “That’s what Second Elder Brother said.”

Shen Rongsheng could not endure another word. He flung back his sleeve and walked out.

chapters.title: I’m Feeding You, So You Eat
chapters.content:
In the cold of winter, the sky darkened early. It was barely past the appointed evening hour, and the darkness had already fallen completely outside.

Shen Weici watched the maidservants bustle about lighting the lamps and crouching before the bronze brazier to replace the charcoal. She shifted her position slightly.

Song Zhang had not returned all afternoon. She had tried to persuade Minhe to take her back, but no matter what she said, he would not let her go. So she had simply waited out the time until now.

She was quietly worried about Yue Deng managing alone, and afraid that the Second Madam might have Yue Deng put to the question.

She was still turning this over in her mind when a maidservant entered and said: “Third Miss Shen, dinner is ready.”

Shen Weici had no appetite at all. The bleeding in her mouth had stopped, but eating would likely pull the wound open again.

She shook her head. “I can’t manage anything.”

The maidservant was at a loss. “Master Qi said the General has given strict instructions that you must eat something. Otherwise the General will be displeased with us when he returns.”

Shen Weici did not want to make trouble for the maidservants over this. She leaned against the bolster and asked: “Is there porridge?”

The girl immediately brightened. “There is lily and lotus seed porridge. Would Third Miss like some?”

Shen Weici nodded. “Just the porridge will do.”

The maidservant went hurrying out and returned with the porridge.

She had thought to feed Shen Weici herself, but seeing Shen Weici reach out and take the bowl, she stood back and waited at the side.

Song Zhang came in from outside to find Shen Weici sitting alone, eating porridge.

She was eating very slowly. She would take a small mouthful, and it would take a long time before she swallowed — as though her throat had only a small opening and nothing could move easily through.

Her outer garment, stained with blood, had been removed, and her hair was down. The dark strands fell loose to her chest and over her shoulders, her face clean and pale, her brows and eyes as though painted by a skilled hand. Even in just a plain, unadorned inner robe she carried that quality of gentle, tired warmth.

It was the kind of thing where the moment you saw her, you felt her warmth wrapping around you.

The collar of her moon-white robe bore faint brownish marks — the traces left from where medicine had dribbled earlier when he fed her.

Song Zhang stood for a moment and then walked over.

He still carried the chill of the outside air on him. He sat down at the edge of Shen Weici’s bed, and then his hand moved with an ease that brooked no argument, lifting the porridge bowl cleanly from Shen Weici’s grip and setting it in his own hands.

He frowned at the small amount remaining in the bowl and looked at her. “Is this all you’ve had?”

The maidservant at the door had already told him: nothing else would go down, only porridge.

Shen Weici still held the silver spoon, her eyes not particularly moved by Song Zhang walking in and simply taking the bowl from her. She knew well enough that this was Song Zhang’s domain.

She glanced at the bowl he had taken — even this small amount had been a struggle to eat.

The wound that had stopped bleeding still carried a faint trace of blood in her mouth.

She gave a deliberately weak cough and said quietly: “I can’t manage it.”

Then she raised her eyes to Song Zhang. “When will Young Master Song let me go home?”

Song Zhang looked at her, then took the spoon back from Shen Weici’s hand, scooped up a spoonful, and held it to her lips, his expression showing displeasure. “You’re that eager to go back?”

Shen Weici said nothing, but cooperated fully — parted her lips and took in what Song Zhang offered, then nodded quietly.

In truth, Shen Weici bore Song Zhang no ill will for bringing her here. He had, after all, helped her — called an Imperial Physician, arranged for maidservants to look after her.

Nor did she particularly wish to speculate on what Song Zhang’s intentions were. Right now, her mind was taken up entirely by worry for Yue Deng.

The people of the Jian’an Marquis household were, every one of them, self-serving to the core. Having their reputation shattered like this, they would be frantic with rage.

Song Zhang saw Shen Weici swallow the porridge down, and scooped another spoonful, holding it to her lips. He watched those exquisitely small lips part and close, that small red mouth barely wider than the spoon itself — full and gleaming.

His gaze deepened as he fed the spoon into her mouth and watched her swallow. His throat moved of its own accord.

His voice came out slightly husky. “I’ll take you back tomorrow.”

Shen Weici heard this and said nothing more. Knowing Song Zhang’s temperament, if she were to open her mouth and ask to leave tonight, this man would likely be displeased. But giving way to his moods, he was not actually that difficult to manage.

She reached out her hands, wanting to take the bowl back from Song Zhang. “I’d better manage it myself.”

They were nominally cousins — something about this arrangement still felt improper.

Besides, Song Zhang had clearly never fed anyone before. He sent spoonful after spoonful with no rhythm at all. Shen Weici’s mouth was aching, and before she had swallowed one she was already looking at the next one offered. It was exhausting — and yet given Song Zhang’s well-meaning stubbornness, she could say nothing.

Song Zhang impatiently held the spoon toward Shen Weici’s lips anyway, his phoenix eyes carrying clear displeasure. “I’m feeding you. You eat.”

Shen Weici blinked, then looked at Song Zhang again. The wound on her tongue had started slowly bleeding again. It wasn’t much, but it couldn’t sustain this rapid feeding.

She was swallowing before she’d fully chewed — it was all she could do to keep pace with him.

Song Zhang watched that vivid red mouth open and close before him and found his body leaning forward of its own accord. He watched her close her lips over the spoon and swallow, and had the sudden, inappropriate thought that he wished he could become that spoon.

He really did want to know what her mouth tasted like. Such a small pair of lips — like a single cherry — and she herself was so gentle and warm. He imagined that the slightest teasing would be enough to bring tears to her eyes.

Shen Weici felt Song Zhang’s body drawing closer. He was already so tall that sitting at the edge of the bed he blocked much of the candlelight behind him. Leaning in as he was, his shadow enveloped her entirely, and the pressure of it seemed to bear down on her too.

Shen Weici looked up in surprise as Song Zhang bent toward her, his burning breath falling against her face.

She lowered her lashes, picked up the handkerchief from beside her, and pressed it to her lips as she coughed — one hand braced on the bed beside her, her body turning to the side.

Her slight frame shivered faintly with the coughing, her fingers at her lips slender and smooth, the pale wrist visible above her sleeve utterly white.

Song Zhang saw Shen Weici begin coughing again so suddenly and checked himself. He quickly reached out a hand and began patting her back. “Why do you keep coughing?”

He saw her turn slightly away from him, her delicate back presented to him, and stood up in exasperation to call for the Imperial Physician again from outside the screen.

But the words were barely out when something light and gentle caught at his wrist guard — he turned, and found Shen Weici looking at him, shaking her head. “I only choked. You were feeding me too quickly.”

Song Zhang paused, then sat back down, his expression cooling. “If I was feeding too quickly, why didn’t you say so?”

Shen Weici lowered her lashes again and said nothing.

Song Zhang realized with some frustration that he was entirely without recourse when it came to Shen Weici. Looking at her lying there weakly, saying nothing, he found every trace of anger in him evaporating and every temper he possessed folding inward.

He scooped another spoonful — less than before — blew on it carefully, and held it to her lips. “Eat slowly. I’m not rushing you.”

Shen Weici had just parted her lips to take it when Minhe’s voice sounded from behind the screen: “General, there is someone here to see you.”

Song Zhang’s gaze remained on Shen Weici’s lips. “Who?”

Minhe’s voice became slightly awkward. “Perhaps the General might step out for a moment, and this one can explain.”

Song Zhang was currently feeding Shen Weici, and had no desire to stop — if he left, he might not have the opportunity again.

He said impatiently: “Just say it.”

From outside, Minhe, hearing this, carefully spoke the words: “It’s Zhang Yuanheng.”

“He says he’s come to see Third Miss Shen.”

chapters.title: Are You That Desperate to See Another Man?
chapters.content:
Minhe’s voice faded. The room went very quiet.

Song Zhang’s face clouded over. Something roiled in the depths of his dark eyes. His gaze landed on Shen Weici.

Shen Weici was equally startled. She had not expected Zhang Yuanheng to come looking for her here, of all places.

He had given no word for so long — had he heard that she was taken away by Song Zhang, and come because of that?

If that was why he was coming to see her now, what did it mean?

But she still wanted to see him. She wanted to ask him why he had broken his promise.

She looked at Song Zhang. His gaze was already on her — unreadable, his deep phoenix eyes carrying something she could only describe as quietly dangerous.

She remembered that Song Zhang had always believed she was the one who had lured Zhang Yuanheng in. Now that Zhang Yuanheng was here, she could only wonder what thoughts were passing through his head.

She did not actually care what Song Zhang thought. But the fact that Zhang Yuanheng had come here suddenly — it had to mean that her father would not allow him to see her at the Marquis household.

And if her father was going to marry her off to Zhang Tingyi, he would obviously want to sever any connection between her and Zhang Yuanheng.

That thought led to another: if she went home tomorrow, she might not be able to see Zhang Yuanheng at all. Her father would certainly have people block any meeting.

But then again — Zhang Yuanheng had returned her keepsakes. Why would he come looking for her after doing that?

There were things that needed to be said and sorted, though. And perhaps saying them here would actually be easier.

She weighed this for a brief moment, then turned to Song Zhang and carefully asked: “Would it be possible for me to see him? Only for a quarter of an hour.”

No sooner had the words left her mouth than Song Zhang’s expression darkened. With somewhat brusque roughness he held another spoonful of porridge out to her and refused flatly: “No.”

He called toward the outer room: “Send him away.”

Shen Weici was briefly surprised, and sat up a little. “Wait —”

She looked at Song Zhang. “Young Master Song, would it be possible to let me see Master Zhang? Just a quarter of an hour.”

Song Zhang heard Shen Weici’s words and felt the veins on the back of his hand nearly rise. He looked at her earnest, pleading gaze — as if she could not wait to see Zhang Yuanheng — and the emotion this stirred in him was deeply unwelcome.

He stared at Shen Weici with cold eyes and said with a chill in his voice: “What do you take this place for — somewhere you meet your admirer?”

Shen Weici had not expected Song Zhang to put it so crudely. Her slender brows drew together slightly. She looked at him and said: “However Young Master Song chooses to speak of me, I will not argue. But Master Zhang and I are finished — there is only something that was left unsaid. I ask that you allow him to enter.”

“It will not take long for Master Zhang and me to resolve what remains between us.”

Song Zhang gave a cold laugh. He set the porridge bowl heavily into a maidservant’s waiting hands, stood, and looked down at her from above — the familiar cold authority back in his phoenix eyes, the fleeting gentleness of a moment ago gone as though it had never existed.

The contempt returned to his gaze, sharp as frost. “Shen Weici, you truly manage to lure men wherever you go. That Zhang Yuanheng comes rushing here the moment he hears you’re in my house — like an obedient little lapdog trailing behind you.”

“Does it give you satisfaction, seducing men? Watching them lose their senses over you — is it something you dream of? Dreaming of becoming the mistress of an Earldom household?”

Shen Weici’s face went white. She looked at Song Zhang with genuine incomprehension. “I truly do not understand what you mean by this, Young Master Song. My acquaintance with Master Zhang came about because my father arranged the match. It was only through that intended marriage that we grew close at all, and our correspondence followed from mutual regard. Every time we met, it was in my father’s study. How does any of that constitute luring?”

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici’s pallid face with cold eyes, the tendons in the back of his hidden hand twitching. He laughed icily. “Lies come so smoothly to you. Do you think I never saw you alone with Zhang Yuanheng?”

“The way you preened and cast meaningful glances at him — and played at warmth and aloofness all at once to keep him obsessed with you — urging him on to come and propose — weren’t those your methods?”

“And I do find myself curious: after all those methods, why hasn’t the man come to propose?”

“He comes looking for you at night, and you can’t wait to see him. You’re lying in the bed I sleep in, wearing nothing but a single inner robe — and you’re this desperate to see some man from outside?”

“Perhaps you’re afraid your hold on Zhang Yuanheng isn’t secure enough?”

Shen Weici’s heart trembled with the force of her anger. She admitted, to herself, that she had used some artifice with Zhang Yuanheng — that she had looked at him with intention in her eyes. But she had also brought sincerity to it, a genuine wish to become his wife.

Her face was white, her voice unsteady. “All I wanted was a secure and reliable match. I once genuinely wished to marry Master Zhang. And yet Young Master Song speaks of me as though I were something shameless.”
