“I would never see Master Zhang in a state like this — I would rise and dress and put my hair up first. That Young Master Song’s mind goes where it does is not something I would have expected.”

Song Zhang’s face hardened. He looked at her trembling eyes, watched her on the verge of tears again — those glistening eyes that made it so easy to believe in her fragility — and the rage in him burned hotter.

Rage at that phrase: genuinely wished to marry.

He sneered. “My mind goes where it does? You know very well what kind of face you have — it makes it trivially easy for you to have Zhang Yuanheng eating out of your hand.”

“The Earldom household is roughly the height you can manage to climb given your standing. Any higher and you couldn’t reach. That’s why you’ve held on to Zhang Yuanheng so tightly — isn’t that right?”

“Clever girl. I underestimated you.”

Shen Weici heard this, closed her eyes, and said no more. She had no desire to speak another word to this man who had decided she was a seductress.

Her position was inherently awkward. She was unwelcome at the Marquis household, and making a good marriage was the one choice open to her. A man like Song Zhang — born to privilege, surrounded since birth by people who catered to him — could never understand her difficulty. Explaining further was pointless.

She had said enough. She would leave it here.

Song Zhang had formed his low opinion of her long ago. The two of them had no real reason to be entangled like this, and yet they kept ending up in each other’s way.

She drew in a slow breath and met Song Zhang’s gaze. “Since Young Master Song finds my presence so unwelcome, I have no right to go on staying here and irritating him.”

Her fingers tightened. Her voice, quiet and wavering, said: “I’ll leave now.”

With that, Shen Weici threw back the quilt and shifted to the edge of the bed. She had barely settled her feet down and begun to reach for her embroidered shoes when a large hand pressed down on her shoulder from above, and she found she could not rise at all.

The weight of that hand was considerable — enough that Shen Weici’s shoulder already ached faintly.

She looked up at Song Zhang in bewilderment. She genuinely could not understand him.

Why was his temper so impossibly changeable?

Song Zhang’s expression had gone to its darkest. The fingers on Shen Weici’s shoulder flexed, and his voice came out cold enough to carry a trace of something alarming: “In my house you see no one and you go nowhere.”

He said this, then released Shen Weici’s shoulder and turned to walk away with long, unhurried strides.

chapters.title: Master Zhang Really Is Single-Minded
chapters.content:
Shen Weici watched Song Zhang go. If it meant he would not return, that would suit her perfectly well.

The entire room was his people. Outside there would certainly be guards. She knew she could not leave right now, and had no inclination to waste the effort trying.

But Zhang Yuanheng knew she was here and had come to see her at night. She suspected there was some misunderstanding involved — otherwise he would have had no reason to come.

She turned and looked out through the window. The shutter had been drawn closed. Below it, a plum branch bloomed, bleak and quiet. She stared at it for a moment, then lay back down on her side, buried in the quilt, exhausted.

She would certainly not be seeing Zhang Yuanheng tonight. She would have to think of another way later.

The maidservant at her side looked at the porridge bowl — still nearly half full — and saw Shen Weici lying down on her side. She asked softly: “Third Miss Shen, would you like any more porridge?”

Shen Weici had no appetite at all. She shook her head.

Her tongue was now a dull, numbing ache. She had spoken so much just now, and the movement had pulled at the wound. She had no desire to open her mouth again.

The maidservant saw Shen Weici’s back turned to her and did not press further. She slipped away quietly.

This Third Miss Shen seemed to be a very good-natured person. All afternoon she had smiled and spoken warmly at every maidservant who approached her — you would never know, looking at her, that this was the woman the General had described as wanton and scheming.

She bowed her head and stepped out, and no sooner had she crossed the threshold than she found the General standing on the covered walkway. His gaze fell on her porridge bowl, and his expression cooled. “That’s all she ate? Nothing else?”

The maidservant nodded quickly. “Third Miss Shen said she couldn’t manage anything else, only porridge.”

Song Zhang’s expression darkened further, the crease between his brows deepening.

Minhe stood at Song Zhang’s side and observed his General’s face, then said quietly: “Shall this one go and send Zhang Yuanheng away now?”

Song Zhang looked at him, then suddenly gave a cold, thin laugh. With a certain detachment he said: “Tell him I was just feeding her porridge, and she doesn’t want to see him. Tell him not to come looking for her again.”

Minhe understood immediately and answered: “This one will go at once.”

Once Minhe had gone, Song Zhang looked at the maidservant again. “Go and bring her some cakes as well.”

With that, he went back to the study.

Out front, Zhang Yuanheng was still standing at the entrance waiting for someone to return with a reply. Under the bright glow of the gate lanterns, seven or eight guards stood in two straight lines on either side of him, and he was finding the atmosphere somewhat uncomfortable.

These past many days, every time he had gone to the Jian’an Marquis household, Minister Shen had turned him away — always saying Shen Weici was resting and could not receive visitors. When he tried to ask about Zhang Tingyi, Minister Shen brushed it off as groundless rumor. He had not known what to do.

He couldn’t very well demand an explanation from the minister.

And at home, for weeks now, his family had been pressing him toward the match with the Song Duke household, leaving his mind in a tangle. He had sent letters that never received replies. He only wanted to see her — to hear one reassuring word from her — and perhaps then he could steady himself.

That object she had returned to him, each time he looked at it, felt like something stabbing at his heart. He had, in the end, broken his word.

She had every right to resent him for it.

Today, when he heard she had coughed up blood, he understood: she was being coerced. Perhaps the returned keepsake had been coerced from her as well.

The Jian’an Marquis household had been keeping him at a distance, blocking every attempt to see her or send a letter.

Now all he wanted, madly, was to see her — to explain himself to her. If she would only believe him still, he would, if necessary, give up his position and kneel before the Emperor to expose what Zhang Tingyi had done.

The great lacquered gate opened again. Minhe walked out, and Zhang Yuanheng immediately stepped forward: “Is Third Miss Shen willing to see me?”

Minhe gave a mild smile and came to stand before Zhang Yuanheng. He sighed lightly. “Third Miss Shen was just in the middle of pestering our General to feed her porridge. When I went in to say so, Third Miss said she didn’t wish to see you — and asked that you not come looking for her anymore.”

Zhang Yuanheng felt as though the ground had shifted beneath him. He swayed slightly, his gaze losing focus. “She truly said that.”

Minhe folded his hands behind his back and regarded the warm, refined man before him with an air of comfortable composure. “Third Miss Shen relies on our General entirely now. And it is only our General who can resolve the business with Zhang Tingyi. What can you offer her?”

“Master Zhang — since Third Miss Shen has asked you not to seek her out, I would advise you to stop going to the Marquis household as well.”

Zhang Yuanheng stared for a moment. This was not right.

Shen Weici would not treat him with such indifference.

And yet he thought back to the day she had returned his things. Did it mean her heart had grown cold?

Because of his broken promise, she had been forced toward a marriage with Zhang Tingyi.

Zhang Yuanheng felt as though his heart were being cut open. Suddenly he could not understand what all these weeks of struggling against his family had been for.

Perhaps it had been for the words she had once said — that she hoped to go with him to see the snow on the spring mountains.

It would not be long before the snow came. He had believed he would be able to take her, properly and openly. Why had so many things gone so wrong?

Zhang Yuanheng shook his head. His eyes reddened slightly. He looked at Minhe: “Master Qi — would it be possible to go back in and pass one more message? Only say that I will see her just this once. If she tells me with her own mouth that she wants nothing more to do with me, I will trouble her no further.”

Minhe sighed. “Master Zhang, why be so stubborn? I’ve heard that the Second Elder Master of the Song Duke household has expressed willingness to form a marriage alliance with the Yiyong Earldom. You should take the opportunity while it’s there. Why hang yourself on one tree?”

“Third Miss Shen is no longer willing to see you. What is the point of pressing on?”

Zhang Yuanheng’s chest ached terribly. All he could remember now was that day by the plum tree — the quiet pavilion on the water, the sound of her voice telling him she was uneasy, that she had dreamed a frightening dream, that she wished to go and see the snow with him, and wished he would come quickly to propose.

But he had broken that promise.

His fingers trembled faintly. He reached into the front of his robe and produced a letter, placing it into Minhe’s hands. “If she is not willing to see me, I understand — and I know it is not her fault. Only please give her this letter.”

He said this and then, with both hands joined together, gave Minhe a deep, formal bow.

Minhe was taken aback. He looked at the letter in Zhang Yuanheng’s hands, then at Zhang Yuanheng bowed before him, and even he — who had seen a great deal — found himself unable to refuse. He accepted the letter.

“I’ll see the letter is delivered. It’s late now — you should head back.”

Zhang Yuanheng looked at the letter in Minhe’s hands and repeated his instruction gravely: “Please make certain it reaches her hands.”

Minhe could not quite meet Zhang Yuanheng’s eyes. “You have my word. Go on home.”

He turned, gave a signal, and had the gate closed. Then he looked down at the letter in his hand — crumpled and slightly worn, as though it had been written some time ago and carried with him ever since.

He thought of Zhang Yuanheng’s wounded expression a moment ago, and exhaled a quiet sigh. He took the letter and went inside.

Behind him, Zhang Yuanheng stood at the closed gate, the cold wind sweeping against him. He remained there a long time, and then, at last, turned and walked away like a man who had lost something irreplaceable.

chapters.title: Kissing Her
chapters.content:
The letter Zhang Yuanheng had given would never reach Shen Weici’s hands. After Minhe brought it back, he handed it directly to Song Zhang.

Song Zhang was leaning back in his sandalwood armchair. The subtle dark-patterned black robe he wore caught the candlelight and revealed faint gold beast designs in the weave. Below the gold coronet, his face was refined and imperious, his phoenix eyes carrying their customary trace of something dangerous and shadowed.

The letter was quickly between his long, slender fingers. Song Zhang looked at the two pages of it and could not help a scoffing laugh.

Zhang Yuanheng turned out to be rather more devoted than he had imagined.

He read the letter through with cold eyes from start to finish. It was, as expected, an explanation for why he had suddenly broken his word and not come to propose. Song Zhang’s gaze settled on the last line, and the curve at the corner of his lips pressed into something hard and cold.

He held the letter over the candleflame and watched it curl into charred ash before letting it go.

He rested one arm lazily on the armrest and propped his temple against his fingers, thinking. Zhang Tingyi was easy enough to deal with. But Zhang Yuanheng with his devotion — that was another matter entirely.

He also thought back to the way Shen Weici had been so insistent just now on seeing him — and the irritation flooded back into his chest.

A guard’s voice sounded outside: “General, Commander Qin of the Jinwu Guard is outside requesting to see you.”

Song Zhang made a sound of acknowledgment. Qin Feng came in.

Qin Feng moved to kneel at the sight of Song Zhang, but Song Zhang gestured and he stopped, placing the items in his hands into Song Zhang’s. “This is the list of names from tonight’s gathering at the Junzi Pavilion, attended by the Fourth Prince and a number of officials.”

He looked at Song Zhang and said quietly: “Men from the Censorate were there as well.”

Song Zhang’s otherwise unhurried expression paused. He raised an eyebrow, then threw the list back down on the table. “Write this up as a memorial for me. I ought to present myself before His Majesty tomorrow.”

Minhe heard this, took up the page, looked it over, and acknowledged the order.

Qin Feng offered another item: a register. “This is the recommended list for the vacancy of Capital Outer Patrol Circuit Commander. Family background, experience, and age are all noted inside. I ask the General to review it.”

Song Zhang told Qin Feng to leave the register on the table, then asked: “Anything else?”

Qin Feng thought for a moment. “All other patrol matters and the rotation of the Palace watch have been arranged to this one’s satisfaction. I would not presume to trouble the General.”

Song Zhang nodded and dismissed him.

After Qin Feng left, Song Zhang reached out and began reviewing the register.

Minhe, reading Song Zhang’s manner, withdrew to a corner without a sound.

In the inner room, Shen Weici had been drifting in and out of a hazy half-sleep when a maidservant’s low voice reached her from behind: “Third Miss Shen, the medicine is ready — it’s time to take it.”

Shen Weici heard her and had to push herself upright to receive the bowl, leaning against the bolster to drink it down.

In the Marquis household, she could always have Yue Deng quietly dispose of her medicine. Here, with a maidservant watching, no matter how bitter it was, she had no choice but to force it down.

This particular medicine was very bitter — bitter enough to make even Shen Weici’s brows furl slightly.

She had barely swallowed the last of the bowl before her hand was over her mouth and she was dry-retching.

The maidservant quickly offered tea. Shen Weici took two sips, and when the taste was sufficiently dulled, she felt somewhat more human.

She asked: “What is the hour?”

“Nearly past the seventh,” the girl said. Then: “Hot water has been drawn. Third Miss, perhaps you might wash up before sleeping.”

Shen Weici looked toward the bedside where two maidservants stood with copper basins, and pushed herself to sit up.

The maidservants moved to wipe her face with a dampened cloth. Shen Weici was not used to being attended by anyone other than Yue Deng, but she supposed they thought her too ill after the coughing of blood to manage it herself, so she endured the help.

After washing her hands and rinsing her mouth, Shen Weici asked all the maidservants to leave, requesting only that one lamp be left at the bedside.

She had eaten almost nothing all day, but she was not hungry. She had been lying down so long that her body felt heavy and soft and drained of energy.

The brazier burned fully in the room, not a sound to be heard — as warm and still as a spring day.

A pleasant fragrance drifted from the incense burner. Through the carved bed-screen she could make out the faint outline of a figure standing watch — the night maidservant.

Shen Weici looked at this for a while. Her eyelids grew heavy, and before she realized it she had drifted back to sleep.

Song Zhang came out of the study when the night was deep. He looked toward the quiet inner room, then walked in with a composed expression.

Minhe, watching this, understood there was nothing more for him to observe, and padded off to bed with a yawn of his own.

Song Zhang lifted the curtain lightly. The maidservant standing guard beside it did not dare make a sound, but reached up and held the curtain back for him, then, catching his single glance, lowered her eyes and retreated to the outer walkway.

The maidservant standing at the bed-screen inside the inner room likewise dared not speak when she saw Song Zhang enter. She bowed her head and slipped out to the front room.

Song Zhang walked to Shen Weici’s bedside. She was deep asleep, still on her side, one pale hand pressed over the quilt, her body curled slightly inward, her long hair spread behind her, covering the entire pillow.

He had seen Shen Weici sleeping several times now, and each time she was the same — face mostly buried in the quilt, only half a pale, small face peeking out, the pointed chin nearly hidden entirely.

He had laced the incense he burned for her with something to help her sleep — he had asked a maidservant to add it specifically for her.

Song Zhang considered her. He knew he was fond of her — had known it to himself for some time. The anger he directed at her was anger that she still thought of Zhang Yuanheng.

He sat his tall frame down, leaned forward, and propped a hand on the bed beside her sleeping face, bending to look at her.

Asleep, she looked even softer — pale and gentle and warm, that vivid red of her lips slightly parted where the quilt had pressed them, the fine curve of her nose catching a point of candlelight.

His gaze drifted downward. Below, the collar of her robe was barely open — well covered, revealing nothing.

Without quite noticing it, Song Zhang’s expression softened. Even the corner of his mouth curved upward of its own accord.

The words he had said earlier were already forgotten. His body bent lower, his throat tightening, his gaze fixed on those lips so close to him. He had wanted to kiss her several times now. Each time, he had not managed it.

This too was taking advantage — she was ill, and he ought not to think such things. And yet his body, the moment it caught her scent, lost any ability to restrain itself.

With one hand he tilted Shen Weici’s chin just slightly, turning that small face toward him. What met his fingers was softness and warmth. Since he was eighteen, he had not kissed a woman. Now his fingers broke into a cold sweat, his breathing tight.

He moved carefully, not wanting Shen Weici to wake and see him in this state of helplessness before her.

Pride had always made it impossible for him to show any vulnerability before a woman.

He had always scorned men like Zhang Yuanheng, who were so besotted with a woman.

In his understanding, women were incapable of anything that mattered. They could not enter the court or lead an army. They could neither bear burdens on their shoulders nor carry loads in their hands. Beyond bearing children, they served no purpose.

His body was already lowering. His lips had reached hers — softer than he had imagined — and with some inexperience he pressed between them, and found his way inside.

chapters.title: One More Kiss — Just One More and Then I’ll Go
chapters.content:
Song Zhang had very little experience.

In the year and more since returning to the capital, many women had pressed themselves against him and offered their lips. But Song Zhang had felt that none of these women were worth touching — felt it would be dirty. The sight of women loosening their robes to flaunt themselves at men had never interested him either.

But Shen Weici was different. She was the only woman who had caught his eye — the only one who appeared in his thoughts repeatedly and would not leave.

She was the only one who, when he came close to her, produced that involuntary pull of wanting to be closer still.

He bent and kissed her. He found the sweet taste there and gradually lost control of himself — moving from some initial nervousness into something he was wholly absorbed by. For the first time he understood what it was that made all the men around him hold a woman and not let go.

Simply kissing her was beginning to feel like it was not enough.

But then he felt Shen Weici’s slender brows draw together, and tasted a thread of blood against her lips — and the thought that had been careening toward somewhere unmanageable was cut sharply short.

Even so, those parted lips were still a temptation. He knew that if he stayed any longer he would lose his grip on himself entirely — and yet at the last he could not hold out against the pull.

Something filled his chest, something without a name.

He drew back his hand and lifted his head to look at Shen Weici. She seemed faintly uncomfortable, the candlelight falling across the beautifully drawn lines of her face.

He had told the maidservant to add a little more of the sleep-inducing incense than usual. Looking at Shen Weici’s face — still no sign of waking — he straightened, allowed himself one long, last look, and then turned and walked out with deliberate steps.

Song Zhang slept that night in the adjacent Yansheng Hall — a small courtyard he used occasionally for quiet moments of leisure, though he rarely came. He had no permanent residence there.

He was burning through the night. He called a maidservant to draw hot water, climbed into the bath, and then looked down into the water. His face arranged itself into an expression of irritation.

Song Zhang was at the height of his vitality. In the military camps, living on the knife’s edge, there had been no room for this kind of distraction. And then an incident involving a woman from the Eastern Lin Kingdom had left its shadow over him, and he had not touched any woman since — not even the ones sent to him.

But since returning to the capital, the Emperor had frequently hosted banquets — occasions with no shortage of women — and over the past year or more, there had been moments of wanting. Nothing as urgent as this, but still.

He closed his eyes and thought of Shen Weici, pressing down a long, controlled breath.

On the other side of the screen, an uninvited maidservant who had not been called in listened to the sounds from within and could not keep her face from flushing, leaning sideways to peek past the screen. Through the rising white steam she could make out Song Zhang’s back, turned away from her — the tan muscles flexing under rivulets of water, that broad back making her eyes fill with a helpless warmth.

Then she observed what Song Zhang was doing and the sound of the water, and found she needed no further imagination.

Her heart pounding like a drum, she reached for the fastenings of her own robe with trembling fingers.

If she helped the General ease this tonight, she would become his woman — and the sole woman in his household.

But her hand had barely moved when a low, suppressed snarl came from within: “Get out.”

The maidservant froze. The General hadn’t even turned his head.

But the menace in that voice drove every last shred of boldness out of her entirely. She scrambled away and fled.

Everyone who served the General closely knew his temper. Once before, a maidservant had tried to slip into his bed while he was drunk. The next instant, she had been kicked clear across the room — several feet from the bed — with ruptured organs, two days of vomiting blood, and a final departure rolled in a grass mat to an unmarked grave.

She quietly counted herself lucky she had retreated in time.

Song Zhang soaked in the water for a long while. Only when the steaming hot water had gradually cooled did he finally step out, his long legs carrying him easily, pulling a cloak around his shoulders as he went.

The maidservants, knowing he would come through, had long since prepared the bed and stoked the charcoal fire.

Song Zhang spent the night in fitful, broken sleep. Shen Weici slept soundly until daylight.

When she woke and found the light already coming in through the windows, she was startled enough to sit bolt upright from the bed.

This was the first time in years she had slept until dawn. Even she was slightly astonished by it — she looked toward the light with a blank mind, not quite present.

She had intended to speak to Song Zhang first thing in the morning about going home. By now he would likely have gone to court, which left the question of when she was going to get back.

She was sitting on the edge of the bed, about to rise, when Song Zhang walked in from behind the carved screen. She blinked, a little vague, and looked up at him. “Hasn’t Young Master Song gone to the Palace?”

Song Zhang came in to find Shen Weici sitting at the edge of the bed in nothing but a single inner robe, her dark hair loose and falling over the white, a few strands having worked their way across her face.

Her small face was faintly pale, but her eyes — catching the shifting light — reflected his own image in them. He found his gaze moving of its own accord to that vivid red of her lips.

He looked at her dazed, upward glance and crossed to her with a frown. “Are you not cold sitting up like that?”

Shen Weici felt somewhat exposed herself in only a single layer of cloth. Her body was a little stiff. She lay back down and pulled the quilt over herself properly, then turned to look at Song Zhang. “Could Young Master Song step outside for a moment? I’ll come out once I’m dressed.”

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. “This is my room. Why should I leave?”

Shen Weici was briefly stopped by this. She did not bother contesting his unreasonable logic. “Once I am dressed, I will not be remaining here.”

Song Zhang looked at her — she seemed to have a little more energy today, her voice somewhat steadier than yesterday’s weakness.

He looked at her all bundled up like a dumpling in the quilt and said with mild displeasure: “I have no designs on you.”

Shen Weici replied plainly: “That was not my meaning.”

Then she asked: “When will Young Master Song take me home?”

This was now the third or fourth time he had heard this question. Did she truly dislike being here with him that much?

His expression flattened. “After breakfast and your medicine.”

Shen Weici heard this and knew better than to press any further.

chapters.title: Song Zhang Discovers Her Secret
chapters.content:
When Shen Weici got up, she asked Song Zhang to go outside first, but he only lolled sideways on the daybed and made no move to leave, his gaze coming to rest on her with that air of lazy indifference.

Shen Weici reasoned that this was Song Zhang’s space, and his temper was not good, and there was no real affection between them — so she said nothing more. She just wanted to tidy herself quickly before he had further occasion for cold remarks.

She asked a maidservant to bring her clothes, then composed herself as best she could and walked past Song Zhang and behind the folding screen.

Song Zhang’s gaze tracked Shen Weici the whole way. In the depths of his phoenix eyes a quiet darkness stirred. Through the thin moon-white of her inner robe, the graceful lines of her body were faintly visible.

A maidservant followed Shen Weici behind the screen to help her dress, and only then did Shen Weici notice that the maidservant was holding different clothes. She asked: “Where is the robe I wore yesterday?”

The maidservant paused, then said quietly: “This one saw that the garment had blood on it, and the General had a new one brought, so I took this one instead.”

Her other robe had a handkerchief in the sleeve — the one stained with vermillion paste. If someone found it, the consequences would be serious.

And returning in a different garment would invite speculation. Going home in yesterday’s clothes, by contrast, would suggest Song Zhang had done nothing especially attentive for her — and that nothing had happened between them.

Shen Weici looked at the maidservant and offered a small, gentle smile. “Please don’t bother with a new one. Just bring me yesterday’s robe — I’ve been wearing that one a long time and am used to it.”

The maidservant hesitated, looking down at the garment she was holding — gold thread on a pink ground with peony embroidery, clearly superior in every way to the bloodstained robe.

After a moment she said: “Very well, Third Miss — please wait a moment while I fetch it.”

She walked out with the new garment.

Song Zhang saw the maidservant emerge with the clothes and frowned. His gaze went back to the slender silhouette visible through the screen.

Before long the maidservant returned carrying Shen Weici’s robe from the previous day, about to pass behind the screen — and was stopped by Song Zhang. “Wait.”

The maidservant stopped short and stood before him, trembling slightly.

Song Zhang said with cool deliberateness: “Who told you to bring that robe.”

But before the maidservant could answer, a gentle voice came from behind the screen: “Don’t blame the maidservant, Young Master Song. It’s my habit to wear my own clothes — I told her to fetch it.”

Song Zhang looked toward the screen with an icy slant to his eyes. “How ungrateful.”

A brief silence from behind the screen, then: “I understand Young Master Song’s kindness, and I am grateful.”

Song Zhang heard that gracious non-answer and gave another cold laugh. Fine — if she wanted the dirty robe, she could have it. What was his concern?

He gestured for the maidservant to take the robe back through.

But as his gaze lowered, he spotted something on the floor — a small square of cloth stained with blood. His mind went to the handkerchief he had seen Shen Weici pressing to her lips the day before.

He looked at it for a moment, then bent and picked it up, holding it at eye level. A faint, metallic smell. But the color of the blood dried on the cloth was not quite right.

Song Zhang had been on the frontier from before he was ten until he was twenty-one. He had seen blood beyond counting. He could tell in an instant that something was off.

His eyes narrowed. He raised it to his nose and drew in a quiet breath — and his expression went cold.

Behind the screen, Shen Weici finished dressing and reached into her sleeve for the handkerchief she had left there the day before. She searched for it for a long moment and could not find it, and her heart gave a quick, uncomfortable lurch.

If that handkerchief were found by someone with a mind to use it, she would have very little to say for herself.

She looked at the maidservant beside her and asked in a low voice: “When you fetched my robe, did you happen to see a bloodied handkerchief?”

The maidservant shook her head, baffled. “I didn’t.”

Shen Weici steadied her expression and nodded, then took the silver hairpin a maidservant offered her and twisted her hair up into a simple knot. She smoothed her sleeves and stepped out from behind the screen.

The moment she appeared, Song Zhang was looking at her — and something in his expression made her unaccountably cold.

She let her gaze move quietly to the floor, found nothing there, then turned her sleeves together and walked past Song Zhang, making her way toward the outer room where clothing was kept.

But she had only taken a step past him when his hand closed firmly around her wrist, halting her. His dark eyes had gone heavy. His face was a mask of ice. Then he raised his other hand and made a gesture, and every servant in the room saw it and lowered their heads, filing quietly out.

In a moment the room held only the two of them.

Behind the daybed a bright window cast light, but Song Zhang’s back was to it, and his expression was difficult to read in the shifting luminance. What was unmistakably clear was the sharp, relentless gaze — the eyes of someone who saw through everything.

Shen Weici looked at the hand locked around her wrist, the grip tight enough to make her wrist ache a little, and felt something quietly drop in her chest. She looked at Song Zhang and said calmly: “If Young Master Song has something to say, there is no need for this.”

Song Zhang’s cold, intent gaze fell on the blood stain at Shen Weici’s collar — genuine blood, the kind she had coughed out before him yesterday. That was real. But what was on the handkerchief she had pressed to her mouth was not blood.

He narrowed his eyes and brought the handkerchief out, a mocking curve at the corner of his lips. “What is this?”

Shen Weici looked at the handkerchief and felt a momentary blank. She had not expected Song Zhang to have found it.

She kept her face composed. She met Song Zhang’s gaze and said plainly: “That is my handkerchief. Not all of what is on it is blood.”

She pressed her lips together briefly. “There is also vermillion paste.”

Song Zhang had not expected Shen Weici to admit it so straightforwardly. He gave a short, contemptuous laugh, his expression cooling again. “You dared to deceive me.”

Shen Weici’s gaze dropped slightly. The quiet in her eyes held a trace of melancholy. She stood still before Song Zhang and said in a measured voice: “I was not deceiving Young Master Song. I did what I did because I had no other choice.”

“My father intends to marry me to Zhang Tingyi, and I do not want that. The blood-coughing was genuine — there simply was not as much of it as it appeared. I only did this to let people see the difficulty of my situation — to let word spread outside, so that my father might be forced by public opinion to reconsider the marriage.”

Shen Weici’s eyes grew faintly wet as she spoke. In the light coming through the window, the moisture made them luminous. Her pale skin, her single silver hairpin — a beauty in tears, without powder or paint, the mountain-and-river softness of her eyes and brows. A single glance conjured fragility and grace.

Her voice came very quietly: “I came to the Marquis household to seek shelter. My days there have not been easy. I have never sought to harm anyone. I only did not want to be married to Zhang Tingyi.”

Song Zhang’s anger had been quietly burning before — furious with himself for being played by a girl. But hearing Shen Weici’s words now, his anger softened against his will.

She was not wrong. All of it had simply been a way to protect herself. He could not really fault her for it.

Besides, her constitution was genuinely poor. He had seen her cough blood with his own eyes yesterday — she had simply seized on it and used it to her advantage.

The cold left Song Zhang’s brow and eyes. The grip around Shen Weici’s wrist eased a little. He looked at her. “Did I not already say I would deal with Zhang Tingyi for you? What are you worried about?”

chapters.title: Everything She Wants, He Will Give Her
chapters.content:
Shen Weici saw Song Zhang’s manner ease and felt a quiet relief move through her. The things she had said — partly true, partly invented — had no real opening for him to pick at, and he appeared to believe her.

She heard his question and dabbed at her eyes with her sleeve, then looked up at him. “Young Master Song was so hard on me before. I simply did not dare trust that he would truly help me.”

Song Zhang snorted. “You think I would lie to you?”

Shen Weici put on a forlorn expression. “Weici knows her own place — she knows she cannot compare to the other young ladies of the Marquis household. She would not presume to expect Young Master Song’s genuine assistance.”

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici’s aggrieved face. It looked like real distress.

He thought back on how he had treated her before — it had not been particularly kind, so it was normal that she would not trust him. Even Song Zhang himself, at the time, could not have explained why he was helping her at all.

He rose from the daybed. His tall frame blocked the light coming through the window behind him, drawing Shen Weici’s small figure entirely into the shadow of his chest.

Song Zhang looked down at Shen Weici. He took in the still-damp fringe of her long lashes, the pink-touched rims of her eyes and the tip of her nose, and found the sight beautiful.

His fingers moved. He suppressed the urge to wipe her tears away himself, and the voice that came out held a warmth he had never used before: “From now on, when you run into trouble in the Marquis household, you may come to me.”

“I am not without some fondness for delicacy. Do you understand?”

Shen Weici found Song Zhang somewhat easier to manage than she had feared. But Song Zhang’s downward gaze made her uncomfortable — his eyes pressed on her face in the same way he had stepped closer and closer to her the day before, until she had feigned a coughing fit to escape.

She turned her head slightly aside, as though abashed, and nodded.

Looking at Shen Weici in this soft, yielding state, Song Zhang could barely contain himself. She was gentle and small and graceful — and only now did he understand in his bones what it was that men found irresistible in a woman: that single tilt of the head with its downturned glance, the shy reserve of a face turned away. No one, he thought, could withstand such a quality of warmth.

No wonder Zhang Yuanheng was so besotted. Even he, standing before Shen Weici, could not keep himself in check. He wanted nothing more than to pull her tight against him and shield her from every harm, to make sure she never had to suffer another grievance.

In this moment, Song Zhang even had a fleeting thought of marrying Shen Weici — of having her follow his every step, lean on him, depend on him — while he gave her all the wealth and status and elevation she could want. Everything she wanted, he would give her.

The memory of her lips beneath his last night moved through him again, and his body inclined toward her before he knew it. He looked at those gently lowered eyes and wanted to take her chin in his hand and kiss her, hard and unrestrainedly, while she looked up at him.

His hand had already lifted.

But Shen Weici, at precisely that moment, bent and reached across to take the handkerchief that he held in his other hand, then looked at him. “May I burn this?”

Song Zhang’s gaze deepened, fixed on Shen Weici’s eyes — innocent and fragile. He pressed his thin lips together, and made a quiet sound of assent.

Shen Weici went to the table, placed the handkerchief against the glass of the candleholder, and watched the flame slowly consume it. Only when the last of it was gone did the weight she had been carrying this whole time fully release.

Song Zhang stood to the side and watched her actions. He came to stand beside her. “I’ll take you home after breakfast.”

He said this and walked past her.

Shen Weici looked at his retreating back, then at the ash on the table. She called a maidservant to sweep it away behind the screen, then followed Song Zhang out.

The breakfast table held more than ten dishes. Shen Weici’s wound had not fully healed and she could not eat much — she simply sat across from Song Zhang and quietly drank her porridge.

Song Zhang frowned at the sight. A constitution this fragile, eating this little — no wonder she coughed blood at the slightest provocation.

He said nothing, his gaze moving to Minhe, who had just come in.

Minhe stepped in and found Shen Weici and the General at the same table, and the shock inside him was considerable — the General had never shared a meal with a woman before, save for elders.

He went to Song Zhang’s side, looked once at Shen Weici, and bent to murmur at Song Zhang’s ear: “Second Madam of the Jian’an Marquis household has arrived. She says she’s come to collect Third Miss Shen.”

Song Zhang glanced at Shen Weici, who was quietly eating her porridge. “Have her wait in the front hall.”

Minhe nodded and went out. He could see that Second Madam had come in considerable force — more than ten maidservants and matrons in her retinue — and seemed determined not to leave without the person she had come for.

When Minhe had gone, Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici. “Your stepmother has come to take you. With whom will you leave?”

Shen Weici had already inferred as much from Song Zhang’s words.

She set down her bowl and looked at Song Zhang. “Would Young Master Song take me back himself?”

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. “If you want me to take you, I’ll have someone send Madam Wen away. Then I can take you back later.”

Shen Weici thought seriously for a moment. Madam Wen coming to fetch her in such haste — the outside rumors must have grown worse, and Madam Wen wanted to put on a performance for public perception. Otherwise she would never have come in person.

But if she did not return with Madam Wen, the Old Madam and Madam Wen would have cause to make trouble for her when she came back later.

She had already worked out her thinking. She looked at Song Zhang. “My stepmother came to fetch me. I do not dare delay.”

Song Zhang gave a short, scoffing sound. “You are always this careful.”

Shen Weici lowered her eyes. “When one has no choice, one is careful.”

Those words — when one has no choice — landed on Song Zhang with an odd weight. He looked at her, quiet and still, sitting there with a peculiar quality of having caught the attention.

He did not trouble her further. His voice came out softly: “Finish eating and I’ll take you over.”

Shen Weici hummed her assent.

She ate without hurrying, finished her porridge bowl, and stopped. She accepted the fragrant tea a maidservant offered and rinsed her mouth politely, then sat in quiet composure, waiting for Song Zhang.

Song Zhang had barely eaten himself, his attention at the corner of his eye following Shen Weici almost the entire time.

When he saw her finished, he rose and brought her toward the front hall.

The walk was silent. Song Zhang walked ahead, his tall frame not moving too quickly — yet Shen Weici’s small steps, hurrying along behind him, had to work to keep pace.

In the front hall, Madam Wen was already seated. When she saw Song Zhang bring Shen Weici in, one in front of the other and Minhe at their side, her expression flickered before she rose and came forward, putting on a show of concern at Shen Weici’s side. “How are you feeling now?”

Shen Weici said carefully: “Yesterday Young Master Song called an Imperial Physician for me and had me take several doses of medicine. I’m much better.”

Madam Wen studied Shen Weici’s face, then noted that she was still in yesterday’s robe — bloodstains at the sleeve and collar, her hair pinned back casually. By all appearances, she had received no particular care here — had not even been given a change of clothes.

She felt her anxiety subside. She had feared Song Zhang was helping Shen Weici, that there was something between the two of them behind her back. Seeing the evidence now, it seemed Song Zhang had simply brought her here as a passing convenience.

She looked at Song Zhang. “Thank you for your trouble. Weici is all right now.”

Song Zhang returned Madam Wen’s gaze with cold indifference, his face expressionless. “I need to be at the Palace shortly. Second Aunt, please see yourselves out.”

With that, he turned and left the front hall without looking back.

chapters.title: Playing a Part
chapters.content:
The moment Song Zhang was gone, the warmth vanished from Madam Wen’s face. Her cold eyes settled on Shen Weici. “When Yen-li came to bring you back yesterday, why didn’t you come with him?”

Shen Weici did not even know that Shen Yanli had come — she guessed Song Zhang must have quietly sent him away.

She looked up with a confused expression. “When the Young Master Song’s people brought me here, I was already unconscious. When I came to again it was nearly midnight. I had intended to come back sooner, but this morning Young Master Song sent word that someone would be taking me home — and then you arrived, so I came with you directly.”

Madam Wen watched Shen Weici’s expression from the moment she came through the door — that same quiet, compliant look, as always. Whenever Madam Wen looked for a place to fault her, there was always a reasonable explanation. It left a chronic, suffocating resentment with nowhere to go.

This whole business had blown up this large because of those two mouthfuls of blood, and she still had not been able to work out how it had come to this.

She pressed her lips tight and said without warmth: “Let’s not discuss this now. Come with me.”

She turned and walked.

Shen Weici watched Madam Wen’s retreating back and followed.

In the carriage, they sat facing each other. The carriage did not go directly back to the Marquis household — it stopped in front of a shop.

Madam Wen’s face was no longer as cool as it had been in the carriage. She turned a warm smile on Shen Weici. “You never have much jewelry on you. We happen to be passing by today — let’s go in and choose a few pieces for you.”

She stepped down from the carriage first and extended a hand toward Shen Weici inside. “Mind your step.”

Shen Weici paused, and understood at once what Madam Wen had in mind.

She wanted to put on a public performance as the warm, charitable Second Madam of the Jian’an Marquis household — she wanted Shen Weici’s cooperation to push back against the rumors.

Shen Weici hesitated for only one moment, then cooperated — reached out and placed her hand in Madam Wen’s.

Madam Wen was being too hasty about this. It would not stop the rumors.

The shopkeeper came forward to greet them. His gaze moved to the bloodstains at Shen Weici’s collar and quickly returned to Madam Wen, smile fully in place. “Second Madam Shen — please come inside.”

Madam Wen linked her arm through Shen Weici’s, her expression warm and unhurried. “Bring out a few fashionable pieces of jewelry. I’d like to choose some for Third Miss.”

People moved in and out of the shop. Outside, the carriage bore the insignia of the Jian’an Marquis household — and those who did not recognize it needed only a quiet word from someone beside them to understand.

The looks that fell on Madam Wen were not kind.

The girl had coughed blood only yesterday. Rather than letting her rest in her room, Madam Wen had her out first thing this morning — putting on a performance. The robe still had blood on it; there had not even been a change of clothes. One glance was enough to see that none of this was real affection.

This was a concubine-born daughter, and she was being worked like she was less than a person.

The woman standing beside Madam Wen was warm and still, extraordinarily beautiful. Both slender brows lowered gently, her cheeks pale, her hands bare — not even a handwarmer, in this cold, after coughing blood. She was bearing up through it.

Meanwhile, Madam Wen was holding a handwarmer herself — pulling a sick concubine-born daughter out to perform for the crowd without a thought for whether the girl lived or died. The falseness of the thing was plain to see.

The looks in the room were all disapproval. It was only when Madam Wen ushered Shen Weici up to a private room on the second floor that the whispers broke out below.

“What a cruel-hearted woman — that poor girl probably won’t last long in her hands.”

“Look at that robe with all that blood — my heart hurts just seeing it. How can she be this pitiable.”

“I heard her coughing again just now. How could she end up with such a vicious stepmother.”

“I think it’s envy — she can’t stand that the girl is better-looking than her own daughter.”

“The Jian’an Marquis household calls itself a distinguished family, but it’s rotten inside. The old grandmother is the same. The Second Madam especially — no one has any respect for her.”

The whispers below spread swiftly through every corner of the street. Madam Wen’s reputation as a cruel stepmother was already set in stone — there was no longer any dissolving it.

In the private room, Shen Weici looked at the box of pieces being pushed toward her, as Madam Wen’s voice came pleasantly: “Take whatever catches your eye. Each season I see to all the girls’ jewelry — yours I take the most care with, before the others have even been seen to.”

Shen Weici understood perfectly that these words were being said for other ears. She played along with polite gratitude: “Thank you, Mother.”

Since Madam Wen wanted her to choose, she looked at the colors and selected a fully green jadeite bangle.

She looked at Madam Wen with a trace of uncertainty. “I don’t have a bangle. Would this one be all right?”

Madam Wen’s face stiffened slightly. The one Shen Weici had chosen was the finest piece in the lot — and the most expensive.

She looked at Shen Weici’s carefully unsure expression, and thought she probably did not know much about jade — and besides, the words had been said. They had been said for other people, and they could not now be taken back.

She kept her smile even. “Whatever pleases you.”

She signaled to the shopkeeper: “This one, then.”

The shopkeeper had brought out these particular pieces specifically because they were the most valuable ones — wanting to see whether this Second Madam would truly part with the money. She had, and he smiled, affirmed the purchase, and quickly went to wrap it.

He had wanted to make this vicious woman spend a little. Looking at the girl who kept her head bowed and did not dare raise her eyes, he felt genuinely sorry for her.

He placed the wrapped box in Shen Weici’s hands and turned to smile at Madam Wen. “Five hundred taels.”

Madam Wen’s expression clenched somewhere inside, but she maintained her composure and had an attendant matron go and settle the account.

After that, Madam Wen took Shen Weici to a cosmetics shop for a round as well — wanting to demonstrate that as stepmother, she had not neglected her charge — quite the opposite.

What Madam Wen did not know was that the people following along behind them had taken everything they’d witnessed firsthand, and turned the rumors into something they’d seen with their own eyes. Her reputation for cruelty was already made, and no amount of shopping would undo it.

Back in the carriage, Shen Weici held the box with the jadeite bangle. She had chosen that piece deliberately.

She had not seen much jade in her life, but she knew enough to know that the greener the jadeite, the more it was worth.

Five hundred taels. That was genuinely no small sum — enough to buy a house and a few shops in a small town like Yuyang.

Madam Wen watched Shen Weici’s hands close around the box, and made a cold, quiet sound. Five hundred taels was not a small sum even to her — but taking the bangle back would hardly be something she, as Shen Weici’s nominal stepmother, could bring herself to do.

She stared at Shen Weici with cold eyes. The marriage to Zhang Tingyi was not going to happen now — but she would not stand by and watch Shen Weici walk into the Yiyong Earldom household as a first wife either.

Her mother had been a low-born creature, and Shen Weici was her mother’s daughter. She would not let her live an easy life. She would never allow her to live better than Zhao-zhao.

She was curious to see what Shen Weici would say when they got back in front of the Old Madam. A punishment was inevitable.

chapters.title: Weici Is Punished
chapters.content:
Back at the Jian’an Marquis Estate, Shen Weici followed Madam Wen first to see Old Madam Shen. Shen Zhaozhao, hearing of their return, came along too. Even the Third Branch had come to get a look.

Shen Weici stood in the main hall and had barely finished her greetings to everyone when Third Branch’s Madam Wang looked at her and said: “Why is she still in the same clothes? Heavens, the blood on that robe — just looking at it frightens me.”

Madam Wen’s expression stiffened at Madam Wang’s words. She looked at Shen Weici. “Now, you explain what happened yesterday. Just how did you come to cough blood?”

Shen Weici had known there would be this accounting. She was about to speak when Yue Deng’s voice, raw with weeping, came from behind her: “Young miss —”

Yue Deng rushed forward and buried herself in Shen Weici’s arms, crying.

Shen Weici, seeing that Yue Deng was unhurt, felt a large measure of relief. She patted Yue Deng’s hand and said in a low voice: “Don’t cry now — I still have to answer the Old Madam.”

Yue Deng heard this and quickly pulled herself back from Shen Weici’s embrace. She saw all the faces above looking down at her with displeasure — obviously censuring her lack of propriety — and used her sleeve to wipe her eyes, then stood obediently behind Shen Weici.

Shen Weici’s account was virtually identical to what Yue Deng had given the night before. The two of them had worked out the story together beforehand. Shen Weici told it more quietly, blaming herself more — saying she ought to have endured longer, she had been too overwrought.

Old Madam Shen heard Shen Weici’s account and in the next moment hurled the teacup in her hand down at Shen Weici’s feet with a crack, her palm striking the table as her voice rose: “You know you should have endured longer?”

“Do you know what your failure to endure has done to this household’s reputation?”

“What it has made of your stepmother and father?”

“Because of these rumors, your father is about to lose his position. And now you stand here telling me you were overwrought. Did you think of the consequences?”

“The first time I could forgive you. But you have now done the same thing twice at a critical moment. This time I will not let it pass.”

“In any case, the marriage to Zhang Tingyi is already dissolved. And since you have done this thing that has damaged the Marquis household’s reputation, I can no longer simply let you go without consequence.”

Shen Weici had already foreseen this on the way back. Old Madam Shen was not going to let her go easily.

Even though, in everything that had happened, she had been the one who coughed blood and she had been the one coerced into a marriage she didn’t want — they would not consider why the household’s reputation had suffered. They would only punish the person easiest to punish.

Shen Weici knew how to make herself small. She did not argue a single point — and besides, her goal had been accomplished.

Under everyone’s eyes, she knelt calmly and composed: “Weici knows she was wrong to cough blood and invite censure. The matter touches the reputation of the Marquis household. Old Madam’s punishment is deserved. Weici accepts whatever Old Madam decrees.”

When those words fell, every pair of eyes in the room went to Shen Weici.

Everyone had expected her to at least argue a little, or cry out a grievance or two. Instead she knelt in silence and accepted the punishment without a word of protest. That was something no one had expected.

Even Shen Zhaozhao stared at Shen Weici with an expression of astonishment. She had completely lost the ability to read this Shen Weici. The girl seemed to always be making herself small and yielding — and yet things always seemed to work out in her favor.

Madam Wang looked at Shen Weici with a trace of sympathy. Still ill, still in a blood-stained robe — and she had to present herself here to be punished. Poor thing.

Above, Old Madam Shen found Shen Weici’s readiness to submit unexpected, and then looked at the bloodstained creases of her robe, and the sympathetic glances the maidservants and matrons nearby were casting in Shen Weici’s direction — and in that moment she felt a faint unease.

She still had many opportunities to put Shen Weici in her place. There was truly no need to do it at the height of these rumors, when it would only reflect on her.

But words already spoken could not be unsaid. Old Madam Shen stiffened her face, thought it over, and then addressed the kneeling figure: “Since you have admitted your fault and accept punishment, you will forfeit three months’ allowance, and during your recovery you will copy out the Women’s Rules fifty times.”

“Do you accept?”

Shen Weici pressed her forehead to the floor. “Old Madam is merciful. Weici accepts.”

Shen Zhaozhao was displeased. She stepped forward and looked at Old Madam Shen. “Grandmother, why is the punishment so light? She has caused the whole of the Jian’an Marquis household’s reputation to be ruined — and she is only being fined three months’ allowance and made to copy out the Women’s Rules? Isn’t that rather lenient?”

Old Madam Shen looked at Shen Zhaozhao. “This mess came from your Second Branch, and your Second Branch can deal with it. I, as an old woman, am only concerned with what is before me. What happens from here is in your mother’s hands. I will have nothing more to do with it.”

Madam Wen heard this and immediately drew Shen Zhaozhao back behind her, then looked at the Old Madam. “Old Madam may rest assured. Something like this will not happen again.”

Old Madam Shen gave a cold snort and said to Madam Wen with deliberate flatness: “Will not happen again?”

“You, as the stepmother, could not manage this small thing properly. The rumors have started because you did not keep order in your own household. From now on, if the Second Branch causes any further trouble, I will simply ask you all to divide the household and go your own way — so you stop dragging the rest of the Marquis household down with you.”

Madam Wang, watching from the side, was quietly gleeful with satisfaction.

She looked at the frightened expression on Madam Wen’s face and said mildly: “Sister-in-law had better manage the courtyard carefully going forward — one must maintain fairness, after all. Otherwise, incidents like this tend to happen.”

“Is that not so, Sister-in-law?”

Madam Wen threw Madam Wang a glare and then replied to the Old Madam: “Old Madam’s teaching is well received. I will take it to heart.”

The words ‘divide the household’ had genuinely frightened Madam Wen.

If the Second Branch left the Jian’an Marquis household, the communal funds would disappear. The shops and farmland allocated in a division would not be generous. Old Madam Shen had always favored the Third Master — kept the best portions for the Third Master because he was infirm. The First Branch had the Commandery Princess to shore it up. The Second Branch, wedged in the middle, received nothing.

Old Madam Shen looked at Madam Wen once more, then gave a weary wave of her hand. “Go. Everyone out.”

Yue Deng saw the Old Madam frown and lean on her matron’s arm to be helped inside. She immediately rushed to help Shen Weici up from the floor.

But just as Shen Weici was about to rise, a pair of embroidered shoes appeared in front of her, and then Shen Zhaozhao’s voice: “Don’t think that because you don’t have to marry Zhang Tingyi you’re going to have a comfortable life. As long as you remain in my mother’s hands, I will not let you live in peace.”

Shen Weici rose calmly and looked at Shen Zhaozhao. “I have heard Second Elder Sister’s words and will remember them. Is there anything else Second Elder Sister wishes to say?”

Shen Zhaozhao was taken aback, then flushed with fury and pointed at Shen Weici. “You actually dare to dismiss me — do you think I can’t do anything to you?”

“Shen Weici, don’t celebrate too soon.”

Shen Zhaozhao could not bear being ignored, and yet every conversation with Shen Weici left her feeling as if she were striking at cotton — she kept losing her temper and wanting to threaten the girl into cowering.

Shen Weici actually had no wish for any great conflict with Shen Zhaozhao. In terms of position, there was an objective difference between them.

Shen Zhaozhao had a childhood sweetheart match awaiting her, and was to marry the heir to the Yong’an Marquis household the following year — a brilliant, elevated marriage. At home she was the sole legitimate daughter, cherished by both the Old Madam and Madam Wen. With everything given to her, why did she insist on treating Shen Weici as a thorn in her side?

Perhaps it was that a life too smooth and perfect, with everything going her way and everyone indulging her, had left no room in her eyes for a single grain of sand.

Shen Zhaozhao’s voice was loud enough that Madam Wang, who had been on the verge of leaving, paused and waited to see what would happen.

Shen Weici looked at Shen Zhaozhao and asked with genuine puzzlement: “Why is Second Elder Sister angry?”

Shen Zhaozhao ground her teeth. “Because you dismissed me.”

At this point Madam Wen came between them, grabbing Shen Zhaozhao by the wrist with a frown. “Zhao-zhao — we are still in the Old Madam’s hall. Stop this scene. Come back with me.”

She glanced at Shen Weici — who was looking demurely at the ground — with a look that was anything but kind, and pulled Shen Zhaozhao away.

Madam Wang saw there was no more entertainment to be had, and regarded Shen Weici for a moment before gathering her sleeves and sauntering out with her maidservants.

Shen Weici was the last to go, and the once-crowded hall fell suddenly quiet.

Her gaze fell quiet as well. As she stepped over the threshold, a voice behind her — Old Madam Shen’s authoritative voice — stopped her: “Don’t think that my failure to punish you severely this time means I have forgiven you. This debt from what you stirred up today is recorded in my ledger. If you make trouble again, don’t expect me to leave you a single shred of dignity.”

chapters.title: Let There Be No Misunderstanding Between Them
chapters.content:
Shen Weici’s step paused. She turned to look at Old Madam Shen standing high above her in the hall — expression stern and cold, sharp eyes seemingly able to see through every disguise she wore.

Shen Weici lowered her gaze. “Old Madam’s words are well taken. Weici will remember them all.”

Old Madam Shen gave a cold sound but said nothing more, only presenting Shen Weici with an indifferent back.

Shen Weici looked at that back for a moment, then turned and slowly walked out.

Yue Deng took Shen Weici’s arm and exhaled with relief. “Did anything happen to you at Second Young Master Song’s place, young miss? I worried about you all day.”

Shen Weici shook her head, then asked: “Did they question you?”

Yue Deng nodded quickly. “Yesterday, the moment I got back, the Old Madam and Second Master both came to ask me. I said everything exactly the way you taught me — they seemed to believe it.”

Shen Weici nodded silently and said nothing more.

When they reached Linchun Courtyard, all the maidservants crowded around with concern. “How is the young miss?”

Then, seeing the blood on her robe: “Young miss, would you like to bathe and change?”

Shen Weici nodded. “Please.”

The hot water was drawn, and while Yue Deng was helping Shen Weici remove her outer robe, she saw Shen Weici take a box from her sleeve. She couldn’t help asking with curiosity: “What’s that?”

“The box looks beautiful.”

Shen Weici placed the box in Yue Deng’s hands. “Five hundred taels.”

Yue Deng nearly dropped it. She clutched it in trembling hands and stared at Shen Weici. “Young miss — did you say five hundred taels? Is there a five-hundred-tael banknote inside?”

Shen Weici smiled faintly. “Open it and see for yourself.”

Yue Deng immediately opened it, and found a deeply green jadeite bangle nestled within — beautiful enough to hold the eye.

“This bangle is worth five hundred taels?” she asked in a shaken voice.

Shen Weici nodded, then smiled: “Keep it safe. In case things at the Marquis household become untenable, or if it’s needed for something, we can convert it to silver. It’s a fallback.”

Yue Deng nodded quickly and hugged the box tight to take it away and put it somewhere safe.

Soaking in the bathing tub, Yue Deng looked at Shen Weici’s back — skin like the finest jade, beautiful in the rising steam.

She also noticed that Shen Weici had been lying there against the tub saying nothing, and hadn’t mentioned what had happened at Second Young Master Song’s place. Yue Deng’s curiosity got the better of her. “Why did Second Young Master Song suddenly carry the young miss off to his place?”

“He looked as though he cared very much about the young miss.”

Shen Weici paused and began to turn over the memories of her time at Song Zhang’s.

The feeling Song Zhang gave her was strange. She had clearly sensed twice that he was moving closer to her — yet his eyes were always cold, and his words still mocking. She genuinely could not imagine what was going through his head.

In truth, she had no real desire to spend much thought on Song Zhang. He was too far removed from her world. Right now, her mind was on Zhang Yuanheng.

She said quietly: “While I was at Young Master Song’s place, Master Zhang came to find me.”

Yue Deng’s hand paused. She looked at Shen Weici’s pale profile. “How did Master Zhang know to come there?”

Shen Weici’s eyes went still. “He must have come to the Marquis household, but Father wouldn’t let him see me — because Father intends to marry me to Zhang Tingyi and clearly doesn’t want me in contact with Master Zhang anymore.”

She exhaled slowly. “I need to find a way to see him.”

Yue Deng was startled. “But he let the young miss down — why does the young miss still want to see him?”

Shen Weici frowned slightly. “I keep feeling there must be some misunderstanding. Master Zhang doesn’t seem like that kind of person.”

Yue Deng said: “But when I went to the Yiyong Earldom household to find him, Master Zhang’s father said outright that Master Zhang had nothing to do with the Marquis household anymore — and that they were arranging a new match for him.”

“Master Zhang said he would come and propose. The family would surely have known. So how could they say there was nothing to do with the Marquis household anymore?”

“It sounded like those words were said on purpose, for me to hear. Does the young miss still think there’s a misunderstanding?”

Shen Weici looked over at Yue Deng. “Was it Master Zhang’s father who told you this?”

“Did you actually see Master Zhang that day?”

Yue Deng looked at Shen Weici’s face, flushed from the steam, and said: “I’d only just arrived at the Yiyong Earldom gate when I ran into Master Zhang’s father coming out. Second Young Master Song was with him — it looked as though Master Zhang’s father was making some kind of apology to people associated with Second Young Master Song. I didn’t understand what it was about.”

“Then Second Young Master Song saw me, and pointed me out to Master Zhang’s father, saying I’d come to find Master Zhang.”

“And then Master Zhang’s father said the Earldom had nothing to do with the Marquis household, and that they were arranging another match, and that if I had anything to say I could say it to him.”

“When I heard that, I was so angry I just handed him everything and left.”

Shen Weici lowered her lashes. “So you never actually saw Master Zhang.”

“But what you said is also true — if Master Zhang’s father spoke like that, the family has clearly withdrawn from the match as well.”

“Even so, I still want to see him.”

“He came looking for me in the night. He must still be thinking of me. Perhaps he even argued with his family on my behalf.”

She let out a quiet sigh: “I shouldn’t have pushed him. But at least I don’t have to marry Zhang Tingyi now, and the matter with Master Zhang can be resolved slowly.”

“But before that, I need to see him. Whatever the outcome, I don’t want any misunderstanding left between us.”

Yue Deng looked at Shen Weici. “Will Second Master still allow the young miss to see Master Zhang now?”

Shen Weici’s eyes shifted. “Let me think.”

Two more days passed. During these days, Shen Weici spent her mornings making pouches and her evenings copying out the Women’s Rules. The Old Madam had given her five days to complete fifty copies — not particularly difficult for her.

That afternoon, Yue Deng was watching Shen Weici sit with her embroidery hoop and could not help asking: “Why is the young miss making so many pouches?”

Shen Weici still had her head bent over the pattern she was stitching. “The Laba Festival is nearly here. I want to give a pouch to each of my cousins and sisters.”

Yue Deng made a face. “The young miss has been here all this time without receiving anything from any of them.”

Shen Weici smiled. “I only want to build goodwill. When I eventually leave the Marquis household and am married, I would like it to be a happy occasion.”

Yue Deng fell quiet and went to help stitch the finished embroidery into pouches. Hexi and Yan’er came over too and sat by the brazier to help.

A while later, a young attendant from Tingzhu Pavilion came to ask Shen Weici to stop by. Shen Weici told him to go ahead and that she would tidy herself and follow shortly.

She asked Hexi and Yan’er to continue with the pouches, then rose and left with Yue Deng.

These past two days, Shen Weici had vaguely sensed that things outside had shifted. She had not gone out of her way to investigate.

These past two mornings when she went to pay her respects, her father had been all worry-creased brows and rushed away quickly. Madam Wen had no patience for conversation either — she had let Shen Weici leave as soon as greetings were over.

The Third Branch’s Shen Mingqiu had even come by once, taken her hand warmly, and told her she’d had good fortune to come through such trouble unscathed.

She made her way to Tingzhu Pavilion at last. She stepped inside softly and saw her father standing with his back to her.

She greeted him quietly. “Father.”

Shen Weici had been carrying a quiet guess about this meeting for some time now. With the rumors outside at this pitch, her father would not marry her off to Zhang Tingyi again. Perhaps to silence the gossip, he might reconsider her match with Zhang Yuanheng.

These past two days she had not brought up the matter to her father herself, because she knew it could only come from him. If she brought it up, she would seem impatient — and her father would think too much into it.

Shen Rongsheng heard Shen Weici’s voice and turned. He looked at the daughter standing before him with her eyes lowered.

Her face resembled her mother’s beautiful face in certain ways. Her nature was gentle and yielding like her mother’s as well.

He found himself thinking of the day Zhang Tingyi came to propose, and what this daughter had said to him then — she had predicted they might face censure, that reputations would be damaged. And she had been exactly right. Now he was tasting the bitter fruit.

From a Fifth-Rank Bureau Director in the Ministry of Revenue, he had been demoted to a Seventh-Rank Chief Clerk in the Court of State Ceremonial — the laughingstock of the entire court. And even now he could not understand how things had gone so far so fast.

This sort of thing was not unheard of. Why, when it fell to him, did the consequences have to be this severe?

What baffled him even more was that yesterday in court, more than half the censors and the men of the upright scholarly faction had knelt to ask the Emperor to severely punish Zhang Tingyi. He himself was from a distinguished family, had passed the imperial examinations through merit, and while he was not one of the common-born purists, he moved in their circles — suddenly finding himself flanked on all sides, with no idea what to do.

The Emperor had suppressed the matter then. But that group had gone and knelt before the gates of the Hall of Diligent Governance, and by afternoon had effectively forced the Emperor to strip Zhang Tingyi of his position. When he heard the news, he had not known whether to feel relieved or to feel his last remaining hope snuffed out.

The feeling had been impossible to describe. The whole affair had been bizarre from start to finish.

It was as though someone had been fanning the flames. And yet it also seemed as though things had simply followed their natural course to this result.

chapters.title: Second Cousin, Why Do You Keep Bringing Up Master Zhang?
chapters.content:
Shen Rongsheng naturally did not believe that Shen Weici — a girl who had only recently arrived in the capital and rarely left the inner courtyard — could have had any hand in this. He simply felt the whole thing was suspiciously odd, and could put his finger on no specific place where it was wrong.

He exhaled a long sigh. The rumors outside were still running wild, and he would certainly not be marrying his daughter off to Zhang Tingyi again.

He looked down at Shen Weici, and his face was tired. “Have you been in contact with Zhang Er-lang these past days?”

Shen Weici shook her head. “From the moment Father told me to prepare for the marriage to Master Zhang, I stopped all contact with Master Zhang and returned everything he had sent.”

She let her gaze drop slightly. “Between Master Zhang and myself — there can no longer be anything.”

Shen Rongsheng heard this and paused, feeling something like guilt.

But he was too dispirited himself right now to take on Shen Weici’s marriage properly. Still, he needed to get her settled — having her well-matched was one way to silence the gossip and demonstrate that the household had not mistreated a concubine-born daughter. Marrying her into the Yiyong Earldom household would, after all, be a respectable match.

He looked at Shen Weici and said in a low voice: “Tomorrow I’ll invite Zhang Er-lang to come by. If he still has intentions, I’ll do my best to settle the matter of your betrothal within these coming days.”

“Prepare yourself for tomorrow.”

Shen Weici heard this, and immediately thought of what Zhang Yuanheng’s father had said. She feared this was not going to be as straightforward as her father imagined.

She hesitated, wondering whether she should tell her father that the Yiyong Earldom was already looking at other matches for Zhang Yuanheng.

She looked at Shen Rongsheng. “Has Father spoken with Master Zhang’s father?”

Shen Rongsheng frowned. “I’ve been too occupied these days — I haven’t been in contact with him.”

“But Zhang Er-lang has always had his own mind about things. If he agrees, the family will likely follow.”

Shen Rongsheng was not particularly worried about Zhang Yuanheng refusing — the young man had still been coming to the household recently, still trying to see Shen Weici, which showed he still had feeling for this match.

And fortunately, he had managed to put Zhang Yuanheng off without an outright refusal. There was still room to maneuver.

Shen Weici said quietly: “In a matter of this importance, Father, it would perhaps be better to first consult the Earldom household as well. Given what happened, they will certainly have their own thoughts. If we proceed without doing so, there is a risk of awkwardness.”

Shen Weici’s gentle reminder landed on Shen Rongsheng. The Jian’an Marquis household’s affair had indeed made a considerable scene — the Yiyong Earldom household would certainly know of it, and Zhang’s family would certainly have reservations. Relying solely on Zhang Yuanheng’s agreement was genuinely not enough — he needed to call on them in person and clear the air, otherwise it truly would become awkward.

He nodded, taking the point. “You are right. I’ll send a calling card to the Zhang household this afternoon. If they write back, it means the matter has room to be discussed.”

“Tomorrow I have to be at my post. If they respond, I’ll ask your stepmother to go to the Zhang household with you and settle this properly.”

“Don’t worry — I’ll instruct your stepmother on what to say at the Zhang household. I’ll do my best to get this match settled for you.”

Shen Weici understood that she could not detain her father, so she nodded docilely. “Very well.”

Shen Rongsheng looked at Shen Weici’s robe and the single thin silver pin in her hair. “Tomorrow, don’t be so plainly dressed. Wear your jewelry — let the Earldom household see that we value you.”

“You are a daughter of the Marquis household. The appropriate presentation matters.”

Shen Weici caught her father’s meaning and nodded. “Father needn’t worry. I won’t embarrass the Marquis household tomorrow.”

Shen Rongsheng felt, somehow, an inexplicable confidence whenever he considered Shen Weici and how she handled things. He nodded as well and let her go.

On the way back, Shen Weici’s heart was faintly unsettled. First, it was Madam Wen who would be accompanying her to the Yiyong Earldom. Second, the Marquis household had been the one to break the agreement first — just thinking about it made her feel she would be in for a round of cold reception.

What had happened was not her doing. But she was the Marquis household’s daughter, and if the matter went smoothly and the match was settled, she would be living as a daughter-in-law in the Earldom household for years to come. She had no desire to leave a poor impression on her future parents-in-law before she had even crossed the threshold.

It was unusual for her to feel this fluttering anxiety.

She did not go straight back to her courtyard. Instead she walked outside for a while and came to sit on a long covered walkway not far from her own quarters, turning sideways to look at the green pond and rockery beyond, deep in thought.

The banana leaf at the edge of the walkway half-concealed her face. The usual warmth of her expression had gone a little cool.

Yue Deng sat beside Shen Weici and said, with some worry: “If Second Madam goes with the young miss tomorrow, will she quietly make trouble?”

“Second Madam certainly doesn’t want the young miss to make a good marriage.”

Shen Weici’s fingers rested against the railing, and her luminous eyes suddenly flicked sideways toward the other end of the walkway, where a dark figure was walking slowly toward them.

She was briefly startled, and thought at once that she should not have come here.

She had no wish to be seen in conversation with Song Zhang out in the open — if any maidservant or bystander caught sight of it, someone would inevitably link it to her being carried off to his quarters, and the resulting gossip would not be pleasant.

Song Zhang moved through any space he occupied and immediately became the center of it. Shen Weici had no desire to become a target herself.

Yue Deng noticed Shen Weici falling silent and asked: “Young miss, why aren’t you saying anything?”

Shen Weici pulled her gaze back and looked out at the surface of the lake, as though she had not noticed the approaching figure. “It’s not as bad as all that.”

As long as Madam Wen had something to be cautious about, as long as she had things she was afraid of, she would maintain at least a surface performance of propriety — she wouldn’t want to validate the rumors with her own behavior.

So long as that constraint remained, it would not be entirely unmanageable.

Before Shen Weici’s words were fully out, before Yue Deng could reply, a footstep sounded close at hand. Yue Deng turned her head a beat too late and found Song Zhang standing beside them, tall and composed.

It was approaching dusk. Winter darkened early. The light was already dimming, though it was only just past the appointed evening hour.

Song Zhang’s face was half in shadow and half in fading light — cold eyes, a thin mouth, phoenix gaze and long brows, a face that in most lights carried a trace of dangerous beauty. He was tall and upright, his expression carrying the contained, pressing weight of someone of authority.

Yue Deng started at Song Zhang’s sudden nearness and quickly called out: “Second Young Master Song.”

Song Zhang spared Yue Deng a single glance, then sat down directly beside Shen Weici. He leaned back, both hands resting on the railing, long legs stretched out at ease, his gaze on Shen Weici. “Zhang Tingyi has been stripped of his position. He can no longer come to propose.”

“I’ve dealt with your trouble. Where is my pouch?”
